title: Sullivan Ranch: xenolith H2O, magma ascent and degassing
text:
1 Summary for co-authors
What has changed in the Sullivan Ranch (SR) work since the 2023 thesis chapter, and what do the new analyses conclude? This document follows the format of the deposited chapter, “Testing the Fidelity of Peridotite Xenoliths as Records of Water in the Lithospheric Mantle”, and leads with what is different. The question is unchanged: do hydrogen (H2O) concentrations in the nominally anhydrous minerals (NAMs) of mantle xenoliths record the mantle, or the magma that carried them up? The data are SIMS and NanoSIMS H2O in olivine, orthopyroxene (opx) and clinopyroxene (cpx) from SR xenoliths and scoria, with melt-inclusion volatiles and the magma’s pressure-temperature (P–T) path. The sections below give the five biggest changes, then an extended abstract that lists every conclusion and major result by stage, then a guide to the chapters. Appendix Appendix E maps all 41 points of the deposited chapter to their present status.

title: Sullivan Ranch: xenolith H2O, magma ascent and degassing
section: 1.1 The five biggest changes since the thesis
text:
1.1 The five biggest changes since the thesis
The changes are ranked by how much they alter the findings. Chapter 2 gives the full ranked table.

The ascent rate is lower and now rests on one history for three minerals (Figure 1.1). The thesis gave 0.2 ± 0.05 MPa/s (isothermal, about 1200 °C) from olivine alone. With temperature falling along the magma’s P–T path, one continuous ascent fits olivine Ol-2, exterior opx and exterior cpx together at 0.100 MPa/s (0.050–0.200 over the temperature-slope envelope), 0.63× the isothermal joint fit of 0.158. That is about 3.6 m/s. The starting melt is the published MiMiC melt; the CO2/Nb start (second scenario) raises every rate by about 10 % (joint 0.112).
The melt degasses water much later than the thesis said. The thesis put the onset of degassing at 150 MPa. The MiMiC starting melt saturates at 682 MPa, but CO2 dominates the early vapor and the melt loses half of its H2O only below about 55 MPa, where the magma is at about 1110–1180 °C. The H2O loss that sets the rate therefore happens at lower temperature than the thesis assumed.
The starting melt is the published MiMiC melt, wetter than the thesis start. The thesis path began from a lava with 3.36 wt% H2O and 8,476 ppm CO2. The new primary start is the published MiMiC melt (Rasmussen et al. 2020) with 3.549 wt% H2O and 8,529 ppm CO2. A second scenario, the CO2/Nb start, has 3.59 wt% H2O and 14,100 ppm CO2 (CO2/Nb 239 × Nb 59) and moves the rate by about 10 %. Intact interior opx cores independently imply 3.48–3.49 wt%, close to both starts.
The fits favor slower pyroxene diffusivities than the 2023 brackets. The 2023 cpx upper bound was extrapolated from Ferriss et al. (2016) to the tetrahedral Al of the WHT1 cpx (they publish laws for Kunlun diopside but no equation for the Al dependence), and the cpx interior profiles used the opx bracket. With the pyroxene diffusivity left free, the fits need slow natural-pyroxene values (log10 D at 1200 °C of −11.0 for opx and −11.5 for cpx), and the pyroxene rates fall from about 0.69 and 0.68 MPa/s (2023) to 0.161 and 0.504 on the path.
The signal reached the xenolith interior through a fast pathway (Figure 1.3). The 2023-style test, in which grain rims sit at the boundary value, fails (χ² 42 for 5 rims). Two standard fits put the network that carries the falling water activity inward at log10 D −6.25 (each grain’s extrapolated rim) to −5.75 (all opx points, one common start, a diffusivity per grain) m²/s at 0.100 MPa/s, 3–9× below the olivine grain-boundary value of Demouchy (2010). This grain-boundary modeling is still in progress (grain sizes and traverse geometry, a path-length factor, the two interior grains at 40.5 and 40.8 mm, and the cpx coupling); the numbers here are the current standard fits.

A sixth change affects the Stage 0 argument: cpx cores hold 1.2–2.6× the H2O that recalibrated experiments predict, so the cpx partitioning check in the thesis does not hold on a common calibration (Chapter 9).

title: Sullivan Ranch: xenolith H2O, magma ascent and degassing
text:
1.3 Extended abstract
What are all the conclusions and major results? They are grouped by the stages of the thesis, from the last event (Stage III) back to the source (Stage 0).

1.3.1 Stage III: after eruption (Chapter 7)
Cooling of bomb-sized xenoliths after eruption does not change the NAM water.

Core concentrations are flat across intact xenoliths of different sizes, and the host’s olivine phenocryst profile survives, which limits any post-eruptive hold at high temperature to well under about 3.6 minutes.
Olivine cores in the xenolith (SIMS dataset, Supplement Table S2: interior 6.89, exterior 5.95 ppm) match phenocryst cores (6.77 ppm), the thesis evidence that the host reset them. The thesis text read about 1.3× higher than the data; the data are unchanged.



1.3.2 Stage II: final ascent in degassing magma (Chapter 8)

Rate. The SR magma decompressed at 0.100 MPa/s on the P–T path (0.050–0.200 over 46–120 °C/GPa), χ² 20.6 for 20 points, against 0.158 for the isothermal joint fit. Olivine Ol-2 alone gives 0.093 (68 %: 0.055–0.154), against 0.143 isothermal and 0.151 for the 2023 fit. The CO2/Nb start gives 0.112 (0.056–0.200).
One history, three minerals. Opx and cpx agree with olivine if their diffusivities are slow (opx −10.98, cpx −11.50). Continuous ascent is best at 82.8 and 120 °C/GPa; at the shallowest slope (46 °C/GPa) a 5-minute stall fits slightly better (χ² 20.3 against 22.0). With the 2023 diffusivities a short stall halved the misfit, but the free-D fit does not need one.
Where the water goes. Saturation is at 682 MPa (922 MPa for the CO2/Nb start); half of the H2O is lost below about 55 MPa (63 MPa). The melt still holds 90 % of its H2O at 248 MPa (340 MPa for the CO2/Nb start).
What moves the rate. The largest choices are the olivine/melt partition coefficient, the diffusivity law (0.13–0.64 MPa/s across laws) and the temperature of loss. The melt-inclusion MiMiC version moves the rates by 2 % or less, and the choice between the MiMiC and CO2/Nb starts by about 10 %.
Among published eruptions (Figure 1.2). SR is 1.0× Seguam 1977, about 0.2–0.3× the subplinian Fuego 1974 and Etna 3930 BP eruptions, and 3.4–11× Cerro Negro, on each study’s own model temperature.
Into the xenolith (work in progress). The exterior opx grain is effectively unbuffered and its rim extrapolates to about zero (−8 ± 42 ppm); the interior grains saw about a fifth to half of the melt’s drop. The two standard fits put the network D at 10^−6.25 (each grain’s extrapolated rim) and 10^−5.75 m²/s (one common start, an opx diffusivity per grain) at 0.100 MPa/s. With the cpx boundary seeing half the network’s drop, opx and cpx fit together, and their fitted common starts (412 and 388 ppm) match the intact interior cores.



1.3.3 Stage I: ascent in water-undersaturated magma (Chapter 9)

Intact interior opx cores (about 411 ppm) are in equilibrium with 3.48–3.49 wt% melt H2O, close to the MiMiC start (3.549 wt%) and the CO2/Nb start (3.59 wt%). The opx traverses sit at two levels: two grains plateau near 300–320 ppm and only the deepest points reach 409–413 ppm. The rate model fits with the MiMiC start (joint χ² 20.6 on the path; it was 41 for the 2.72 wt% mixture start with the CO2/Nb-start fit (the mixture start shares the CO2 of the CO2/Nb start)); the offset is stated as uncertainty in the opx partition coefficient or in the starting H2O.
Fe–Mg diffusion gives Ol-2 a residence time of 18.4 days (15.7–21.3) at 1250 °C in the final melt, and xenocrysts 0.15–3.0 days. The two localities (pit and roadside) were probably two magma pulses.
Cpx cores hold 1.2–2.6× the H2O that recalibrated experiments predict. Wetter magmas carry wetter xenolith NAMs (SR, Vulcan’s Throne), drier magmas drier ones (Cima).



1.3.4 Stage 0 and implications (Chapter 10)

No vestige of mantle water is demonstrated in these xenoliths: the interior cores record the host melt, as the thesis concluded. The cpx partitioning misfit is an open caveat.
Published xenolith-NAM ascent rates assume a fixed zero boundary from entrainment, so they are upper bounds and not like-for-like with melt-based rates.
The thesis’s accelerating-ascent picture (0.002 MPa/s deep, 0.2 MPa/s shallow) now reads 0.1 MPa/s in the upper crust; the deep rate is not recomputed.



1.3.5 Inputs and data quality (Chapter 4, Chapter 5, Chapter 6)

The SR melt inclusions record primary melt batches (H2O follows Cl); their CO2 was largely lost before trapping (retained 9–54 % at CO2/Nb 239). Inclusion saturation pressures are 129–574 MPa, shallower than pickup at about 1.15 GPa.
A total 1σ replaces the deposited combined uncertainty, which was about 0.58× the 1σ; six analyses fall below the detection limit.
Two thesis table errors are corrected: GC2_ol4 carried GC2_ol3’s volatiles, and the Fig. 11 caption printed 0.009 ± 0.003 for the olivine partition coefficient 0.0009 ± 0.0003.

title: 2  What changed since the thesis
text:
2.1 Problems with the 2023 methods and the fixes
Which differences between the 2023 chapter and the present analyses change the findings, and by how much? Table 2.1 lists the twelve largest, ordered by consequence for the conclusions. The sections after it explain the problems with the 2023 methods and how each was fixed, then list the new analyses and the new direction.
The full 41-row comparison with the deposited chapter is in Appendix E.
What was wrong with the original analysis, and what replaced it? Seven problems matter.
The pyroxene diffusivity bracket. The 2023 fits bracketed the pyroxene diffusivity with laws at T ± 20 K. The upper cpx value in that bracket was extrapolated from Ferriss et al. (2016) to the tetrahedral Al of the WHT1 cpx; they publish laws for Kunlun diopside but no equation for the Al dependence. The cpx interior profiles were fit with the opx bracket, and the opx interior profile of GCB duplicated the WHT1 exterior profile. These diffusivities are faster than the fits now need, which made the pyroxene rates (0.69 and 0.68 MPa/s) disagree with olivine. Leaving D free gives opx −10.98 and cpx −11.50 in log10 m²/s at 1200 °C, matching slow natural-pyroxene values, and a joint χ² of 20.6 for 20 points.
Isothermal 1200 °C. The thesis modeled the whole ascent at 1200 °C. Along the P–T path the melt is at 1110–1180 °C where most H2O leaves, so the isothermal diffusivity is too high. The path rate equals an isothermal fit at about 1150 °C, the mean entrapment temperature of the SR inclusions.
The degassing path start. The 2023 path began from the GCB lava and implied no water loss until 150 MPa. The MiMiC start saturates at 682 MPa and loses half of its H2O only below about 55 MPa (CO2/Nb start: 922 and 63 MPa). It still holds 90 % of its H2O at 248 MPa (CO2/Nb start: 340 MPa). The 2023 path is reproduced exactly with its own inputs, so the difference is the start, not the code.
SIMS combined uncertainty. The deposited combined uncertainty (about 0.58× the 1σ) understated the error on each H2O value. A total 1σ combining calibration, counting and background replaces it, with detection limits and quantification limits per session. One cpx value (T1-216) was re-reduced on the opx line (129.70 against 131.26 ppm).
The olivine partition coefficient prior. The MATLAB prior was N(9, 0.5) × 10⁻⁴, with an SD 6× narrower than the ±0.0003 in the source paper. The mean is unchanged, and the wider range lets K move the rate as it should (K = 6 raises it 2.29×; K = 12 lowers it 0.58×).
GC2_ol4 volatiles. The 2023 inclusion table gave GC2_ol4 the volatiles of GC2_ol3 (H2O 2.39, CO2 3,136 ppm before correction). GC2_ol4 has no measured volatiles and is now excluded from the inclusion tables.
The Fig. 11 caption. The caption printed the olivine/melt partition coefficient as 0.009 ± 0.003, ten times the 0.0009 ± 0.0003 the scripts and text use.

text:
2.2 New analyses
Which analyses did the thesis not have? The list below names them; each is developed in the chapter shown.

A temperature path from the mantle start to the surface, with the rate warped onto it (Chapter 8, Appendix A).
A joint fit of olivine, opx and cpx with free pyroxene diffusivity, and a stall test (Chapter 8).
Fe–Mg residence times with FORSTER for Ol-2 and the xenocrysts (Chapter 9).
Coupled and nested grain-boundary fits, with buffering of exterior grains (Chapter 8).
Original and modified MiMiC runs and the CO2/Nb estimate of undegassed CO2 (Chapter 6, Appendix B).
Alternative olivine laws, edge treatments and solubility models (Appendix A, Appendix C).
A like-for-like comparison with published rates on each study’s own model temperature (Chapter 8).
Detection limits and the total uncertainty for every H2O value (Appendix D).

title: 2  What changed since the thesis
text:
2.3 New direction
Where does the work go from here? The working hypothesis is that the host magma resets the NAMs, so the xenoliths record the ascent and not the mantle. The interior opx cores equal the MiMiC melt within about 2 %, and the data constrain how fast the host’s falling water activity is transmitted inward. Three consequences follow. Temperature along the path is part of the rate, not a footnote. The fits are joint, so one ascent must explain olivine, opx and cpx at once. The next tests are the partitioning of cpx, the CO2/Nb scenario and the starting level of the opx (Chapter 11).
Sources: report/appendices/c-ch3-crosswalk.md, docs/ASCENT_RATE_SUMMARY_2026-10-22.md, docs/MODEL_CHOICES_2026-10-21.md, docs/supplement/SUMMARY_WRITEUP_NOTES.md.

title: 3  Introduction
text:
3.1 The four stages on the 2026 path
Do hydrogen concentrations in xenolith minerals record the mantle, or the magma that carried them up? Peridotite xenoliths are used to estimate water in the lithospheric mantle, which matters for viscosity, melting and electrical conductivity. Laboratory work shows that H+ diffuses fast in olivine, cpx and opx, so a mineral can equilibrate with its carrier melt in hours. The thesis chapter asked whether that happens in nature, and tested it against the carrier magma’s own pressure, temperature, water content and degassing path. This report keeps that question and updates the answer.
How does the ascent divide into stages for H? The thesis used four, and Table 3.1 places them on the present P–T path. The magma leaves the last mantle equilibration at 1330 °C and 2.26 GPa (Plank and Forsyth 2016), picks up the xenolith at about 1.15 GPa, saturates at 682 MPa (MiMiC start; 922 MPa for the CO2/Nb start), and loses half of its H2O only below about 55 MPa (63 MPa) (Figure 3.1).
The stages differ in what they let a xenolith record. In Stage I the melt is undersaturated, nothing leaves it, and the NAMs track its H2O. In Stage II water leaves the melt and the boundary value drops, so the outer parts of the crystals lose H. The profile length scale gives the time, and so the rate. The next section explains why Sullivan Ranch can test this.

title: 3  Introduction
section: 3.2 Why Sullivan Ranch can test it
text:
3.2 Why Sullivan Ranch can test it
What makes this cone a good test? The cone in the Uinkaret field north of the Grand Canyon supplies every part of the system at one eruption.

Xenoliths of different sizes: bombs GCB1, WHT01 and WHT06 give olivine, cpx and opx, and WHT1 has grains at 0.5, 7.5 and 40 mm from the xenolith exterior.
Melt inclusions: 12 SR inclusions give the melt’s H2O, CO2, trapping pressure and temperature.
A phenocryst, Ol-2: a scoria olivine profiled along [100] gives the rate without a xenolith.

The samples come from two localities, a pit (WHT06, AZ18-06 inclusions) and a roadside (GCB1, WHT01, GC2 inclusions), probably two magma pulses. The path is kept SR-wide. Vulcan’s Throne and Cima, separate volcanoes with drier melts, are used only to test the cpx partitioning, never for the rate.

title: 3  Introduction
text:
3.3 What each later chapter answers
How does the report move through the evidence? Chapter 4 describes the samples and models, and Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 give the NAM and melt-inclusion results. The discussion then follows the thesis order. Chapter 7 asks whether post-eruptive cooling matters. Chapter 8 gives the rate, the one history that fits three minerals, and how the signal entered the xenolith. Chapter 9 asks whether the minerals reset to the host and for how long. Chapter 10 asks what survives of the mantle water, and Chapter 11 lists what is not determined. The next chapter, Chapter 4, sets out how the data were measured.
Sources: docs/plans/2026-10-29-report-review.md, report/appendices/c-ch3-crosswalk.md, data/supplement/summary_csv/.

title: 4  Samples and methods
text:
4.1 Localities and samples
Which samples were measured, how were water and major elements quantified, and which models turn the profiles into a rate? This chapter gives the samples (Table 4.1), the SIMS and EMPA methods (Table 4.2), the melt-inclusion treatment, and one paragraph on each model. Detail sits in the appendices: diffusion in Appendix A, melt inclusions in Appendix B, degassing in Appendix C, and data quality in Appendix D.
The xenoliths and scoria come from three alkali-basalt cinder cones in the Uinkaret and Cima volcanic fields: Sullivan Ranch (SR), Vulcan’s Throne and Cima vent 16. SR is a cone south of Mt. Trumbull, sampled at two sites that probably record different magma pulses. The pit on the cone flank gave WHT06 and its scoria in place, and the roadside gave the weathered-out bombs WHT01 (also written WHT1) and GCB1. The roadside scoria holds Ol-2, the olivine whose profile sets the ascent rate. Vulcan’s Throne and Cima serve only as comparison volcanoes. All SR ascent-rate work uses SR alone. The SIMS dataset (Supplement Table S2) has 284 analyses, of which 270 are accepted.
The roadside scoria AZ09-GCB supplies the GC2 inclusions and a whole rock that is somewhat altered; the AZ09-UK01 lava is the Fe/Mg reference and the starting composition for the degassing paths. Bombs were chosen because they cool faster than xenoliths in lava; one lava-flow xenolith (CA18-Lavablock) tests the cooling rate. SR xenoliths were sectioned and polished as thick sections; Cima and Vulcan’s Throne xenoliths were crushed and clusters hand-picked, so their position in the xenolith is unknown. Samples were cleaned in acetone, toluene, distilled water and isopropanol baths, with only acetone-soluble plastics in preparation. The Sullivan Ranch material is the same cone that earlier work called Trumbull, GC2 and GCB; this report uses the name Sullivan Ranch.

title: 4  Samples and methods
text:
4.2 Water by SIMS and NanoSIMS
Water was measured in three sessions: the Cameca 6f at the Carnegie Institution for Science in 2013 (Cima and Vulcan’s Throne) and 2018 (GCB1 and its scoria), and the Cameca NanoSIMS at Caltech in 2020 (WHT01 and WHT06, mounts A and B). The 2013 session could not measure olivine reliably above background, and the 2020 session had too high a background, so 48 of the 52 accepted olivine analyses are from 2018 and the other four are Cima olivine below the detection limit. Samples were mounted in indium, held at 90 °C under vacuum for 2 days, and kept under ultrahigh vacuum (10^-9 Torr) for 72 hours before analysis. A Cs+ beam measured 16O1H, 12C, 19F, 31P, 32S and 35Cl relative to 30Si.
Calibration. Each session has one line per phase from standards run in the same session: H2O (ppm) = slope × (16O1H/30Si × SiO2 wt%) + intercept, fitted by orthogonal-distance regression with bootstrapped uncertainties. The opx line uses the revised KBH-1 value of 202 ppm (±15; 217 before), which scales earlier opx concentrations by 0.93. Olivine is reduced on the opx line in all sessions. That puts the olivine data within about 12 % of the Withers (2012) olivine line, and the olivine/melt partition coefficient K = 9 ppm per wt% (Towbin et al. 2023) was built on the same scale, so data and K share one calibration. Placing olivine exactly on the Withers line would be equivalent to K of about 10.1 and would lower the isothermal Ol-2 rate from 0.155 to about 0.125 MPa/s. One NanoSIMS opx (T1-216, in Cima) was re-reduced on the opx line, giving 129.70 ppm against 131.26 ppm as deposited.
Uncertainty. Each analysis carries a total 1 sigma, the square root of the summed squares of the calibration term (the larger side of the 5–95 % calibration interval divided by 1.645), the counting error and the blank scatter beyond counting. It replaces the deposited combined uncertainty, which understated the calibration term. The median total 1 sigma is 0.34 ppm for olivine (SR olivine at most 0.59 ppm; the four Cima olivine about 2.9 ppm), 11 ppm for opx and 22 ppm for cpx. The four Ol-2 spots carry 0.31–0.43 ppm.
Detection limits. For each line, L_C (decision limit) and L_D (detection limit) follow Currie (1968) from the scatter of Suprasil blanks beyond counting statistics, and LoQ is the concentration at 20 % relative uncertainty (Table 4.2). Six accepted values lie below L_D (four Cima olivine and two Cima cpx from CA18-05x) and two lie between L_D and LoQ (SR scoria cpx xenocrysts). Every SR olivine value (2.2–8.7 ppm) is above the 2018 LoQ of 1.44 ppm.

title: 4  Samples and methods
text:
4.3 Electron microprobe
Major elements were measured on the Cameca SX100 at the American Museum of Natural History in 2018 (GCB1) and on the Cameca Tactis over several sessions from 2020 to early 2022. EMPA supplies the SiO2 used in the SIMS reduction, the Mg# and tetrahedral Al of the pyroxenes (used in the cpx partitioning test), and the olivine Fo profiles. Phases were assigned by composition (cpx CaO of at least 15 wt%; opx CaO below 3 wt% and MgO 28–37 wt%). Mg# is molar with all Fe as FeO. No usable EMPA exists for several Cima and Vulcan’s Throne grains and for the WHT06_2 xenolith, so those cpx have no tetrahedral-Al value.

title: 4  Samples and methods
text:
4.4 Melt inclusions
Inclusions are naturally glassy and olivine-hosted, hand-picked from the SR scoria (AZ18-06 from the pit and AZ09-GCB from the roadside), the Cima scoria MO10-16 and the Vulcan’s Throne scoria. Glass H2O and CO2 were measured by SIMS, and major elements by EMPA. Seven SR inclusions also have LA-ICP-MS trace elements [CHECK: LA-ICP-MS instrument and protocol are not in the sources read]. Twelve SR inclusions are used; GC2_ol4 has no measured volatiles, and GC2_ol6 is excluded because its glass is too magnesian for its host, which points to olivine in the analysis.
Overlap correction. For AZ09-GCB and Vulcan’s Throne, the SIMS volatiles are the Plank-lab values corrected for beam overlap with the host olivine (factors 1.14–1.67, with Cl corrected further by 1.239). This is not the correction for post-entrapment crystallization. The formula is the Plank lab’s [CHECK: formula and its source]. The AZ18 inclusions carry the revised SIMS H2O and CO2 and new EMPA analyses; Cima values are uncorrected.
MiMiC. MiMiC (Rasmussen et al. 2020) adds or removes host olivine until each inclusion is in Fe–Mg equilibrium with its host (Kd from Toplis 2005; Fe3+/FeT fixed at 0.2 for SR), then adds back the CO2 that the vapor bubble holds with a bubble-growth model. The published code takes the bubble CO2 volume from a Redlich–Kwong pure-CO2 fluid scaled by the CO2 mole fraction; two errors in it partly cancel. The production run replaces this volume with the Duan and Zhang (2006) H2O–CO2 mixture at MiMiC’s own vapor composition. For the SR inclusions the change adds 0 to 15 % to bubble CO2 and raises the saturation pressure with bubble CO2 (Pvbg) by 0 to 7.6 %, and it leaves every inclusion H2O unchanged. The inclusion tables use the production run. The P–T path keeps the base (published) MiMiC, because the two give the same path: a slope through the inclusions of 98.5 °C/GPa (68 % range 89.1–108.5) with the base run and 98.3 with the Duan and Zhang run, and entrapment temperatures differ by at most 1.2 °C. Other options, including a Fe-loss correction and other solubility models, are in Appendix B.

title: 4  Samples and methods
text:
4.5 Models
Degassing path. The path of melt H2O against pressure is a closed-system MagmaSat path at 1200 °C on the AZ09-UK01 lava composition (Fe3+/FeT 0.167). The primary start is the published MiMiC melt, 3.549 wt% H2O with 8,529 ppm CO2, which saturates at 682 MPa (Chapter 6). On this path the melt loses half its H2O only below about 55 MPa. The second scenario, SR-1 (the CO2/Nb start), is 3.59 wt% H2O with 14,100 ppm CO2; it saturates at 922 MPa and loses half its H2O below 63 MPa. Iacono-Marziano is the alternative solubility model and gives a lower saturation pressure (Appendix C).
P–T path. Temperature falls along a straight line from 1330 °C at 2.26 GPa (Plank and Forsyth 2016) to the surface, with a slope drawn from U(46, 120) °C/GPa. This is equivalent to an isothermal fit at about 1150 °C, the mean SR entrapment temperature. The isothermal 1200 °C fit is kept as the simple case.
Diffusion fits. Pressure falls linearly in a one-dimensional slab whose rim holds the equilibrium H2O of the degassing melt (Appendix A). The Bayesian fit returns a posterior median and 68 % range for the rate. Olivine uses the Ferriss et al. (2018) [100] law, D = 10^-5.4 exp(−130 kJ/RT) m²/s, with K = 9 ppm per wt%. Pyroxene K is anchored on opx: Novella et al. (2014) multiplied by 0.93 gives 117.7 ppm per wt%, and cpx K follows the measured cpx/opx core ratio. A temperature that falls along the path enters through a warped pressure, the integral of D(T)/D_ref over pressure, so the constant-D solver gives the variable-temperature result exactly and reproduces the isothermal fits when the ratio is 1.
Joint fit. One continuous ascent is fitted to Ol-2 and to the WHT1 exterior opx and cpx together, with the pyroxene diffusivities free. Stalls are tested against it.
Xenolith exchange. A nested model lets each WHT1 pyroxene exchange with a grain-boundary network of diffusivity D_gb whose water activity follows the melt at the xenolith exterior, with a boundary-drop factor g for each position. It is fitted to all five WHT1 traverses, with the D_gb activation energy set to 34 kJ/mol (Demouchy 2010).
The next chapter turns to what the SIMS data show in each mineral.
Sources: data/supplement/summary_csv/ (Samples, Calibrations, EMPA, Melt_Inclusions); docs/supplement/SUMMARY_WRITEUP_NOTES.md; the deposited Chapter 3 Methods.

title: 5  Results: water in olivine, cpx and opx
text:
5.1 Olivine
What do the SIMS data say about water in the xenolith minerals, mineral by mineral and volcano by volcano? Only accepted analyses are used (270 of 284; the 14 flagged or excluded rows are listed in the data workbook). Table 5.1 gives the ranges, and the sections below follow the thesis order: olivine, cpx, opx, then the contrast between volcanoes.
Olivine at the 1–10 ppm level is at the limit of existing techniques, so the quality of the measurement matters here more than for pyroxene. Every SR olivine value is above the 2018 quantification limit (1.44 ppm), and the median total 1 sigma is 0.34 ppm, so the 2–3 ppm differences between rims and cores are real. Earlier infrared work on SR xenoliths reported 11–16 ppm in olivine (Li et al. 2008), higher than any SIMS value here [CHECK: the infrared and SIMS scales were not compared in the sources read]. The Cima olivine, measured in 2013, are all below L_D, so they bound the olivine water at a few ppm and nothing more.
Olivine holds 2.2–8.7 ppm in SR, almost all of it measured in 2018 on GCB1 and its scoria. The cores in the GCB1 xenolith interior hold 4.3–8.7 ppm (mean 6.9, n = 8) and the cores at the exterior 4.8–7.7 ppm (mean 6.0, n = 9). The scoria phenocryst cores hold 5.9–7.9 ppm (mean 6.8, n = 5). The interior and exterior cores overlap within their scatter, and both overlap the phenocrysts, so the cores across the xenolith and in the host magma have equilibrated to the same water content (Figure 5.1).
Every olivine is zoned, with lower water in the rim. Xenolith rims average 4.6 ppm (n = 13) and phenocryst rims 3.6 ppm (n = 3), and the lowest rims, at the xenolith exterior and in phenocrysts, hold 2.2–3.6 ppm. Rims sit 1.8 ppm below cores in the xenolith and 3.2 ppm below in the phenocrysts, so the zoning is stronger in the phenocrysts, where the rim is closer to the melt. The two populations still share their core concentrations and the same zoning length scale of about 100 µm.
Ol-2 is the phenocryst whose profile sets the ascent rate (Chapter 8). Its four spots along [100] rise from 4.43 ppm at 23 µm from the rim to 5.34 at 56 µm, 7.38 at 117 µm and 7.87 at 154 µm, each with a total 1 sigma of 0.31–0.43 ppm. The profile drops by about 44 % over 150 µm, which is the signal that the diffusion fits explain. Ol-6, a xenolith olivine, drops from about 7.7 ppm in its interior to 5.4 ppm at 19 µm (Figure 5.1 c).

title: 5  Results: water in olivine, cpx and opx
text:
5.2 Clinopyroxene
The pit and roadside cpx overlap: the WHT06 cpx are not zoned at the resolution measured (cores 346 ppm, rims 368 ppm, two analyses each), while the roadside xenoliths differ in how much water their cpx hold, GCB1 being the wettest.
SR xenolith cpx hold 206–488 ppm. The GCB1 cpx hold 373–488 ppm (mean 440), the WHT01 cpx 206–438 ppm (mean 315) and the WHT06_1 cpx 312–400 ppm (mean 340). At conventional SIMS resolution GCB1 cpx rims are only slightly below cores (exterior 430 against 453 ppm; interior 415 against 449 ppm). The NanoSIMS profiles, with a spot every 5 to 10 µm, show the zoning clearly (Figure 5.2). The WHT1 exterior cpx falls from 355 ppm at 98 µm from the rim to 206 ppm at 26 µm, a drop of 42 %. The WHT1 interior cpx-2 falls from 404 ppm at 96 µm to 285 ppm at 7.5 µm, a drop of 30 %. One exterior cpx, close to the xenolith edge (1.45 mm in), is flat at 293–316 ppm. So the cpx close to the xenolith exterior record water loss at the rim, but not all grains do.






Figure 5.2: Pyroxene rims hold less water than cores in every group, and the deficit is largest at the WHT1 exterior (opx rims at 0.49 of the core mean). (a, b) Cpx and opx cores (filled) and rims (open) against distance from the xenolith exterior, GCB1 and WHT1. (c) The two WHT1 exterior profiles the rate fits use, against distance from the crystal rim.

title: 5  Results: water in olivine, cpx and opx
text:
5.3 Orthopyroxene
Opx water is similar to cpx water at the same xenolith, with most SR opx cores between 290 and 360 ppm. The pit xenolith WHT06_2 holds the highest value, 507 ppm, from a single analysis in one grain, so it is not treated as a typical core.
SR xenolith opx hold 96–507 ppm. In both xenoliths with opx traverses, the cores at the xenolith exterior hold less than those in the interior: 292 against 356 ppm in GCB1 and 290 against 359 ppm in WHT1. The two large interior WHT1 opx, about 40 mm from the exterior, reach 413 and 409 ppm at their deepest points. These values anchor the wet starting melt, but the other points of these grains sit lower, near 300–320 ppm (Chapter 9).
Zoning is stronger in opx than in cpx and spreads farther into the grain. The WHT1 exterior opx at 0.5 mm from the xenolith edge rises from 96 ppm at 21 µm from the rim to 315 ppm at 172 µm. The exterior opx at 7.5 mm rises from 158 ppm at 19 µm to 264 ppm at 105 µm. Exterior rims average 142 ppm in WHT1 against interior rims at 265 ppm. Water loss in opx therefore reaches about 100–170 µm into the grain, deeper than the 100 µm in cpx, and it is clearest at the xenolith exterior. Not every GCB1 opx shows it: the exterior opx rims there (268 ppm) sit only 24 ppm below the cores (292 ppm).
Opx and cpx in the same xenolith track each other. The cpx/opx core ratio is 1.38 in GCB1 and 0.97 in WHT1, so the two pyroxenes appear to share one reservoir. The olivine/opx core ratio in GCB1 is 0.018, so olivine holds far less water relative to pyroxene than the experiments would give at equilibrium, which fits olivine re-equilibrating with the melt after the pyroxenes (Chapter 8).
crumbs: 5  Results: water in olivine, cpx and opx

title: 5  Results: water in olivine, cpx and opx
text:
5.4 Between volcanoes
The three volcanoes differ in xenolith water. SR cpx (mean 349 ppm, 206–488) are about three times wetter than Cima cpx (mean 113, 64–198), and SR opx (292 ppm) are about 3.6 times wetter than the four Cima opx (81 ppm). The melts differ in the same direction: the best melt H2O is 3.55 wt% for SR (3.59 wt% with the H2O lost to the bubble) and 1.29 wt% for Cima (Chapter 6). Cima olivine is below the detection limit, so no olivine ratio is given.
Vulcan’s Throne breaks the simple pattern. Its xenolith cpx (264–594 ppm, mean 421) are wetter than SR’s and overlap GCB1, although its best melt, 2.29 wt%, is drier than SR’s. The cpx therefore do not scale with melt H2O across all three volcanoes: the cores hold 1.2 to 2.6 times the water the recalibrated experiments predict, with Cima closest to prediction and Vulcan’s Throne farthest. Wetter magmas still carry wetter xenolith NAMs between SR and Cima, and drier magmas drier ones; the Vulcan’s Throne excess is tested in Chapter 9. Scoria cpx phenocrysts are far drier than xenolith cpx at each volcano (Vulcan’s Throne 35–65 ppm; SR phenocryst cores 74 ppm), as expected for crystals grown from the degassed melt.
Analyses flagged as bad were not used (14 rows: 6 SR olivine, 4 SR opx, 3 SR cpx and 1 Cima cpx).
The profiles above say how water left the grains; the next two chapters give the melt it left for, starting with what the inclusions record (Chapter 6) and then the ascent that the olivine profile measures (Chapter 8).
Sources: data/supplement/summary_csv/ (NAM_Volatiles, NAM_Summary, Magma_Models); the deposited Chapter 3 Results.

title: 6  Results: melt inclusions and the starting melt
text:
6.1 What the inclusions record
What do the melt inclusions record, and which melt should the ascent models start from? Twelve SR inclusions are used: five from the pit scoria (AZ18-06 Ol19, Ol21, Ol23, Ol35, Olxx), the Ol36 pair from the pit, and five from the roadside scoria AZ09-GCB (GC2_ol3, ol5, ol7, ol8, ol11). The sections below show what the inclusions record, how much CO2 the melt had already lost, how the two sites differ, and the starting melts built from them (Table 6.2).
The spread in inclusion H2O is a property of the trapped melts, not the result of H loss. H2O in the measured glass rises with Cl (r = +0.90) and S (+0.86) across the 12 inclusions and is not ordered by entrapment pressure (+0.29, p = 0.37; Figure 6.1). Degassing removes S before H2O and H2O before Cl, and Cl is so soluble in mafic melt that it seldom leaves until very low pressure, so a tight H2O–Cl correlation cannot come from degassing or from diffusive H loss. The simplest reading is batches: a wet, Cl- and S-rich, low-SiO2 melt and a drier, more siliceous one, either mixed or trapped separately. With ten main-group inclusions this is a lean, not a proof. A size test agrees: Ol21 should re-equilibrate 3.3 times faster than Ol23 if H were being lost through the olivine, yet their H2O (3.47 and 3.55 wt%) agree within 2 %.
Plotted together, the three volcanoes keep their separate fields (Figure 6.2). SR inclusions are wetter than Vulcan’s Throne’s, which are wetter than Cima’s. The Duan and Zhang bubble correction shifts bubble-corrected CO2 by only −2.8 to +14.8 % across 39 inclusions, so the pattern does not depend on the equation of state.

title: 6  Results: melt inclusions and the starting melt
text:
6.2 CO2 lost before trapping
Every inclusion trapped a melt that had already lost CO2. Bubble-reconstructed CO2 reaches 9,079 ppm (GC2_ol7; 8,529 ppm in the published MiMiC run, which is the primary start), and the saturation pressures with bubble CO2 are 129–574 MPa, far shallower than xenolith pickup at about 1.15 GPa. The melt’s own Nb gives the undegassed amount: CO2 equals CO2/Nb times Nb, and the lava has 59 ppm Nb. The depleted-mantle ratio of 239 (Saal et al. 2002) gives 14,100 ppm, and the ocean-island ratio of 505 ± 168 (Rosenthal et al. 2015) gives 29,800 ppm. Every inclusion lies below both, and with each inclusion’s own LA-ICP-MS Nb and the ratio 239, the melts had lost 46–91 % of their CO2 (36–77 % on the lava Nb with ratios of 239–673). The same inclusions had lost at most 0.21 wt% H2O to a CO2-rich vapor before trapping (median 0.05 wt%), because H2O stays in the melt at those pressures. Measured CO2/Nb is 21–130, which is 0.05–0.58 times 239; this independently shows CO2 degassing before trapping and rules out an over-corrected bubble. CO2/Ba was tried as the tracer and rejected, because SR Ba/Nb is 11.5–16.5, far above that of the reference pairs.
Whether the CO2/Nb correction is worth making is a question for co-authors (Chapter 11). It moves the rate by about 10 %, because CO2 sets only where degassing starts, and the H loss that the profiles record happens below about 60 MPa. It matters for depth: the CO2/Nb 239 start saturates at 922 MPa, close to pickup, and the 505 start at 1,438 MPa, deeper than pickup.

The roadside GC2 inclusions are drier than the pit inclusions at the same host Fo, lower in Cl and S, and trapped deeper (Table 6.1). Published MiMiC (primary). Ol23 holds 3.549 wt% H2O after correction for crystallization (3.55 in the production run). With the CO2 of GC2_ol7 (8,529 ppm) it gives the as-trapped melt, which starts the degassing path partway down at 682 MPa (708 MPa for the production run). The 2023 start (3.36 wt%, 8,529 ppm, published MiMiC on the 2023 inputs) gave 0.141 MPa/s.

The MiMiC start is supported by more than the inclusions. If the host magma reset the xenolith pyroxenes, the intact WHT1 opx cores (about 411 ppm) record the melt they equilibrated with, and the opx-anchored K (117.7 ppm per wt%) gives 3.48 wt%, within 2 % of the MiMiC start (3.549), within 3 % of the CO2/Nb start and well above 2.72. The joint rate fit with the MiMiC start has a chi-square of 20.6 on the path, against 41 for the mixture with the CO2/Nb-start fit. The opx plateaus near 300–320 ppm complicate this, because they equal the mixture with the same K (Chapter 9).
Where the inclusion values come from matters less than it may seem. The production and the published MiMiC change every rate by 1.4 % or less, because the saturation pressures differ by a few percent and H loss happens at low pressure. The 2026 input changes (revised pit SIMS and a corrected Ol36_2 CO2) move the pyroxene rates by up to 4.4 %, more than the code does (Appendix B). The choice between the two CO2 starts moves the rate by about 10 % and the mixture by up to 21 %, more than either.
The melt that the models start from is now fixed, and the next chapters use it: Chapter 7 covers the eruption and Chapter 8 the ascent in degassing magma.

title: 7  Stage III: after eruption
text:
7.1 What cooling and holds can do
Could a hold at the surface, or the cooling of a bomb, have made the water profiles we use for the ascent rate? The answer is no for the rate, and probably no for the xenolith water contents. Stage III is placed first because it is the last process that could have changed the minerals, and it has to be excluded before the earlier stages are read from them.
Stage III starts when the bomb leaves the vent. The mineral rims keep losing water until the crystal cools below its closure temperature. Two properties of the system limit how much they can lose. First, a bomb of this size cools in minutes, and its exterior, where the profiles used for the ascent rate sit, quenches fastest. Second, a xenolith holds only about 10 % vein and film melt and a few percent vesicles, so after the surface quenches there is little water-bearing phase in contact with the grains, and transport along the veins and boundaries slows as it cools. The thesis tested this with the two xenoliths of different size: if cooling mattered, the larger one (WHT1) should have drier interiors than the smaller (GCB1) while their exteriors match. The exteriors and interiors of WHT1 clinopyroxene are all drier than those of GCB1, but orthopyroxene, which diffuses faster, shows no systematic difference, so size does not order the water contents [CHECK: the thesis comparison is qualitative; no new size test has been run].

title: 7  Stage III: after eruption
section: 7.2 How long a hold would the profiles allow
text:
7.2 How long a hold would the profiles allow
A hold or a cooling ramp acts as extra time at the eruption temperature. For cooling at a constant rate \(c\) from 1200 °C, the time-equivalent hold at 1200 °C is \(R T^2/(E_a c)\), with \(R\) the gas constant, \(T\) the starting temperature in kelvin and \(E_a\) the activation energy of the diffusivity. Table 7.1 gives the result for the three minerals. Even at 1 K/s the equivalent hold is 2 to 3 minutes, and at 10 K/s it is 11 to 18 seconds.



Table 7.1: Cooling at 10 K/s or faster is equivalent to a hold of under 20 s at 1200 °C, far below the 3.6-minute olivine reset time. Time-equivalent hold at 1200 °C for each mineral, for constant cooling from 1200 °C; activation energies are the ones in the column heads.

The olivine phenocryst Ol-2 sets the tightest limit. A core of this size resets in \(r^2/D \approx\) 3.6 minutes at 1200 °C, and the Ol-2 profile still has a core above its rim values, so any post-eruptive hold must be well under 3.6 minutes. Cooling at 1 K/s would use 139 s, about 0.64 of that time, so the profile would be marginal. Cooling at 10 K/s or faster is negligible. The measured quench rate of these bombs is not in the sources [CHECK: bomb-exterior cooling rate]. The pyroxene cores take longer to reset (14 minutes for cpx and 34 minutes for opx with the 2023 diffusivities), so their profiles tolerate a longer hold still.
The direction of the error matters as well as its size. A post-eruptive hold lowers every apparent rate relative to the true one, because the profile has had extra time to diffuse. It cannot make the ascent look faster, and it cannot explain why the pyroxenes gave faster rates than olivine when published diffusivities were used. The joint fit in Section 8.3 resolves that disagreement through the pyroxene diffusivities, so no hold is needed.
With the surface excluded as the source of the profiles, the next question is what the profiles say about the final ascent in the degassing magma (Chapter 8).
Sources: docs/ASCENT_RATE_SUMMARY_2026-10-22.md (post-eruptive cooling table), report/chapters/06-ascent-rates.md (reset times), the thesis Discussion (bomb size and cooling).

title: 8  Stage II: final ascent in degassing magma
text:
8.1 Where the melt loses its water
What does the water zoning in the olivine phenocryst and in the xenolith pyroxenes say about the last stretch of the ascent, and how did that signal get into the xenolith? This chapter answers it in seven steps. We first find where the melt loses its water, then fit the decompression rate to the olivine phenocryst Ol-2 with temperature falling along the magma P–T path. We then show that one ascent history fits olivine, orthopyroxene (opx) and clinopyroxene (cpx) together, rank the choices that move the rate, test the constant-rate and starting-CO2 assumptions, place Sullivan Ranch (SR) among published eruptions, and finally ask how the degassing signal travelled into the xenolith. Stage II is the part of the ascent where the host melt exsolves most of its water and the mineral rims lose water in response.
Over what pressure range does the SR melt actually lose its H2O, and so over what range can the mineral rims record it? The answer fixes which part of the ascent the profiles can resolve.
The starting melt is the published MiMiC melt (Rasmussen et al. 2020, base run: 3.549 wt% H2O from inclusion Ol23, 8,529 ppm CO2 from GC2_ol7; Chapter 6). MagmaSat in a closed system saturates this melt at 682 MPa. The melt then loses little water for a long way: it still holds 90 % of its H2O at about 248 MPa, 1.86 wt% at 60 MPa and half of it (1.77 wt%) at 55 MPa. Three quarters is gone by about 16 MPa, and at 10 MPa only 0.70 wt% remains, 20 % of the start. Most of the water therefore leaves in the last 55 MPa. At the joint-fit rate of 0.100 MPa/s (below), those 55 MPa take about 9 minutes, against about 3.2 hours for the whole interval from the 1.15 GPa pickup pressure to the surface at the same constant rate. The caveat is that this CO2 is the melt as trapped: the inclusions had already lost 46–91 % of their CO2, so the MiMiC path starts partly degassed, shallower than xenolith pickup. The second scenario, the CO2/Nb start (3.59 wt% H2O, 14,100 ppm CO2, CO2/Nb 239 × Nb 59 ppm), saturates at 922 MPa and loses half its H2O below 63 MPa; it is the case for an undegassed melt and is developed below as an option.
The shape of the path depends on the solubility model more than on the start. At 10 MPa, MagmaSat gives 0.67 wt% and Iacono-Marziano 0.92 wt% for the CO2/Nb start (SR-1), and the olivine rate on the Iacono-Marziano path is 0.086 MPa/s, 0.55 times the MagmaSat rate (both isothermal at 1200 °C, CO2/Nb start); the MiMiC start would scale both by about the same factor. We use MagmaSat as the primary model and treat Iacono-Marziano as a sensitivity case, because only the isothermal olivine fit has been run on it. The other degassing choices move the shallow path little. Open-system instead of closed-system degassing leaves the melt 0.05 to 0.07 wt% wetter at 10 MPa. Starts from 2.2 to 3.6 wt% H2O differ by 0.04 to 0.08 wt% there. Evaluating solubility at the path temperature changes every rate by 3 % or less (Appendix C).
Figure 8.1 shows where along this path the melt-equilibrium value of each pyroxene falls below the measured rims. Ten of the twelve exterior rims cross it below 126 MPa, and the WHT1 rims between 13 and 116 MPa; the outermost WHT1 opx rim (96 ppm) is reached only at 13 MPa. The two GCB1 cpx rims sit above the starting level and never cross. The rims therefore record the shallow part of the path, below about 125 MPa, where the melt loses most of its water.
Temperature enters because the path from the 1330 °C, 2.26 GPa mantle start (Plank & Forsyth 2016) cools as the magma rises. With the median slope of 82.8 °C/GPa the path is at 1147 °C where the melt has lost half its H2O (55 MPa) and 1142 °C at the surface. Both are well below the 1200 °C used in earlier isothermal fits. The next section shows what that does to the rate.

title: 8  Stage II: final ascent in degassing magma
section: 8.2 The decompression rate from Ol-2 on the P–T path
text:
8.2 The decompression rate from Ol-2 on the P–T path
What decompression rate does the olivine phenocryst Ol-2 give once temperature follows the magma P–T path instead of staying at 1200 °C? Ol-2 is the one profile that sits fully in the melt, so it sets the absolute rate.
Ol-2 comes from the GCB1 roadside scoria and is normally zoned from a Fo 88 core plateau to Fo 84 at the rim. Its H2O profile of four points (4.4 to 7.9 ppm, outermost point 23 µm from the edge) runs along [100], the same line as its electron-microprobe traverse. We fit it with the Ferriss et al. (2018) [100] diffusivity, \(D = 10^{-5.4}\exp(-130\
\mathrm{kJ}/RT)\) m²/s (\(10^{-10.0}\) m²/s at 1200 °C), and the Towbin et al. (2023) olivine/melt partition coefficient K = 9 ppm per wt%. The boundary follows the closed MagmaSat path from the MiMiC start, and the fit uses the Bayesian grid posterior of the earlier work (Appendix A).
Variable temperature adds no new solver. For continuous ascent the profile depends on time only through \(\int D\,dt = (D_{ref}/v)\int r\,dP\), where \(r = D(T)/D(1200\ °\mathrm{C})\). A constant-diffusivity fit run on the warped pressure \(P_w = \int_0^P r\,dP'\) therefore gives the variable-temperature solution, and its rate is the true ascent rate. With \(r = 1\) the fits reproduce the isothermal ones exactly, and a direct implicit solver agrees with the warped model to 0.02 wt%, the same difference the two solvers show at 1200 °C. The path is a straight line from the mantle start with a slope drawn uniformly from 46 to 120 °C/GPa. That envelope spans the Towbin & Plank (2026) range and a Monte Carlo line through the start and the 12 SR melt inclusions (98 °C/GPa, 68 % range 89 to 109).
The result is 0.093 MPa/s (68 % range 0.055 to 0.154), or about 3.4 m/s at 2,800 kg/m³. That is 0.65 times the isothermal 1200 °C fit (0.143 MPa/s, 0.108 to 0.193), and 0.62 times the 2023 thesis fit (0.151 MPa/s), which is itself within 6 % of the new isothermal value. With the CO2/Nb start the same fit gives 0.101 MPa/s (0.060 to 0.167), 0.65 times its isothermal 0.155. Figure 8.2 shows how the rate depends on the path slope, and Table 8.1 gives the simple and best rates for all three profiles.






Figure 8.2: The P–T path lowers every rate by nearly the same factor, so it moves the absolute rate but not the disagreement between minerals. The cooling path is the largest single shift in the rate, and it lowers it. The reason is that the melt loses most of its water below about 60 MPa, where the path is at 1100 to 1180 °C and the isothermal fit overstated the diffusivity. A path through the SR inclusions (98 °C/GPa, the coolest family) gives 0.070 MPa/s (0.050 to 0.099), 0.49 times the isothermal rate, and the Towbin & Plank (2026) slopes (46 to 90 °C/GPa) give 0.120 (0.082 to 0.176), 0.84 times. The SR-wide envelope between them gives the 0.65 headline factor. The path rate equals an isothermal fit at about 1150 °C, which is also the mean entrapment temperature of the SR melt inclusions.
Every mineral slows by almost the same factor because their activation energies are similar (olivine 130, opx 144 and cpx 115 kJ/mol). The path therefore does not change the disagreement between minerals. With published pyroxene diffusivities the opx rate is 1.7 times and the cpx rate 5.4 times the olivine rate on the path. The change from the 2023 values for the pyroxenes (opx 0.690 to 0.256, cpx 0.678 to 0.728 isothermal) comes mostly from the 2026 degassing path, which keeps more water late, and from the opx-anchored K (117.7 ppm per wt%, against the 2023 prior of 90): with the 2023 diffusivity brackets these alone moved the opx rate about 2× down and the cpx rate about 1.4× up. The pyroxene disagreement is resolved in the next section through the diffusivities, not through the history.
Two checks on the olivine edge treatment leave the rate where it is. Widening the prior on the final pressure from 0–5 to 0–200 bar moves the isothermal rate only within 0.143 to 0.152 MPa/s (run on the CO2/Nb start, 0.155 to 0.164 MPa/s, and scaled by 0.92). A two-population model, with mobile and trapped H as in Barth-type edge locking, fits Ol-2 only if the trapped H exchanges within about 10 s, and it then reduces to an effective diffusivity; slow edge locking cannot remove the roughly 75 % of its H that Ol-2 lost. With the absolute rate set by olivine, the pyroxenes can be added to the same history.

section: 8.3 One ascent history fits olivine, opx and cpx
text:
8.3 One ascent history fits olivine, opx and cpx
Can a single continuous ascent explain the water profiles of olivine, opx and cpx together, once the pyroxene diffusivities are allowed to differ from the 2023 values? It can, and the diffusivities it needs are those of slow natural pyroxenes.
The joint fit uses Ol-2 (4 points), the WHT1 exterior opx (6) and the WHT1 exterior cpx (10), 20 points in all. The olivine diffusivity is fixed at the Ferriss [100] law, and the opx and cpx diffusivities are free. The history is either continuous ascent or a fast ascent to a stall, a hold of 0 to 10 minutes, and a final ascent. We also ran the 2023 method on the pyroxenes: each profile gives the pyroxene diffusivity it needs for the olivine rate, with a wide flat prior, and the joint fit agrees with it (Appendix A).
With the 2023 pyroxene diffusivities held fixed the best joint χ² was 150 to 500 for 20 points, and the cpx carried most of the misfit. With the diffusivities free, the continuous isothermal ascent gives χ² 20.0 and the headline fit on the P–T path gives 20.6 (Table 8.2). That path fit puts the joint rate at 0.100 MPa/s, with a range of 0.050 to 0.200 over the slope envelope of 120 to 46 °C/GPa. It is 1.1 times the olivine-only value (0.093 MPa/s) and 0.63 times the isothermal joint rate (0.158 MPa/s), so adding the pyroxenes changes the olivine answer by about a tenth. Olivine carries 13.3 of the 20.6 χ² units, cpx 6.3 and opx 0.9. The olivine profile alone, with its four points, reaches χ² 6.0 in its best isothermal fit on its own (CO2/Nb start), so the joint fit costs olivine some fit quality to match the pyroxenes.

The pyroxene diffusivities at 1200 °C stay at \(10^{-11.0}\) m²/s for opx and \(10^{-11.5}\) m²/s for cpx whichever temperature treatment is used, because the published laws shift with temperature by the same factor as the fit. Figure 8.3 compares them with published laws. The opx value (−10.98) is within 0.12 log units of the Carpenter (2003) [100] law for San Carlos enstatite (−11.10). The cpx value (−11.50) lies at the slow end of the published cpx laws, between the natural Cr-diopside laws and the slowest Kunlun diopside laws of Ferriss et al. (2016): the nearest faster law is their 3540 cm⁻¹ band (−11.31, 0.19 log units faster), then the slow natural Cr-diopside laws (Ingrin et al. 1995, −11.12; Hercule & Ingrin 1999 uptake, −11.17), about 0.35 log units faster. It is about 7 times faster than the Ferriss et al. (2016) bulk-H law for Kunlun diopside. That suits the SR pyroxenes, which carry 3.3 to 3.9 wt% Al2O3 and Cr-bearing diopside. The faster laws for Al-poor enstatite (Demers-Roberge et al. 2021, −10.21 to −9.75) would need an olivine rate 7 to 20 times faster.






Figure 8.3: Only slow laws for natural, Al- and Cr-bearing pyroxene match the diffusivities that the olivine rate and the joint fit require. Implied log10 D at 1200 °C of opx and cpx from the olivine rate (circles: median; bars: 68 % and 95 %) and from the joint fit (diamond), against published laws evaluated at 1200 °C.



The 2023 cpx bracket is faster than these fits need. Its upper bound, \(10^{-6.71}\exp(-100\ \mathrm{kJ}/RT)\), was the thesis estimate for a cpx with 0.07 tetrahedral Al, extrapolated from Ferriss et al. (2016). They publish laws for Kunlun diopside but no equation for the dependence on Al; the estimate’s prefactor matches their 3540 cm⁻¹ band law (log D0 −6.7) and its activation energy their bulk-H law (100.4 kJ/mol).
The exterior opx and cpx are not a like-for-like pair, and this pushes the cpx rate up. The modeled opx sits 0.5 mm from the xenolith exterior, the modeled cpx 7.5 mm (±2 mm) in. The opx rims across WHT1 show that the melt’s water drop reached that depth only in part. Rim/core is 0.31 at 0.5 mm and 0.60 at 7.5 mm, where an opx shares the cpx’s position, and 0.51 to 0.83 at 40 mm. The exchange fit puts the boundary drop at 7.5 mm at 71 to 83 % of the melt’s by the end of ascent (Section 8.7).
A boundary that drops less than the melt leaves the grain wetter than a melt boundary predicts. A cpx fit with the melt as its boundary therefore needs less time and returns a faster rate, so position pushes the cpx in the observed direction. The size is modest. On the grain-boundary boundary the implied cpx diffusivity moves by 0.03 to 0.06 log units, about 1.1 times on the rate. At the strongest buffering the cpx profile allows it moves by 0.35 log units, 2.2 times. That covers part of the 5.4-fold gap between the cpx-only and olivine rates, and the rest still needs the slow cpx diffusivity. Position is also not the only control on cpx loss. The second exterior cpx, 1.45 mm from the exterior, has no rim gradient: it is flat at 260 to 310 ppm, 0.67 to 0.80 of the intact cores, across its whole 130 µm traverse. It either lost water throughout or started lower. The exterior opx is effectively unbuffered. Buffering makes a pyroxene-only rate too fast, so the implied diffusivities are, if anything, lower bounds.
A stall is not needed at the central slope. With the 2023 diffusivities a short stall of under 2 minutes halved the misfit, but with the pyroxene diffusivities free the continuous ascent is the best history at 82.8 °C/GPa (a tie, χ² 20.6 against 20.7) and at 120 °C/GPa (worse by 3.6 for the best stall). At the coolest slope (46 °C/GPa, rate 0.200 MPa/s) a 5-minute stall fits better (χ² 20.3 against 22.0), and in the isothermal fit a stall does not help (20.2 against 20.0). A single stall improving one slope by 1.6 does not justify the extra parameter. A deeper stall would also push the pyroxenes slower than olivine, the wrong direction. The next section asks which choices could still move the rate.

title: 8  Stage II: final ascent in degassing magma
text:
8.4 What moves the rate
Which modeling choices change the olivine rate, and by how much? The answer ranks the uncertainties that could change the headline rate and shows which of them we have excluded.
Table 8.3 lists the choices, sorted from the largest increase to the largest decrease. The factors are relative to the isothermal CO2/Nb-start rate of 0.155 MPa/s (the MiMiC start gives 0.143, a factor of 0.92), and the path rows apply to the best fit. The two rows from Section 8.5 are relative to the CO2/Nb path rate (0.101 MPa/s). The factors were computed on the CO2/Nb start; because every rate scales by about the same 0.92 with the MiMiC start, the factors carry over. Three groups stand out.

Choices that lower the rate: the diffusion temperature (0.49 to 0.84 times) and the solubility model (Iacono-Marziano, 0.55 times).
Choices that can raise it by factors of 2 to 4: the olivine diffusivity law and the olivine partition coefficient K. The wrong crystal axis would lower it by factors of 16 to 32.
Choices that move it little: the starting H2O, the solubility temperature and the melt-inclusion software version (12 % or less). A higher starting CO2 raises the rate by up to a third.

If the ascent accelerated toward the surface, the rate the profile records over the last 60 MPa falls by up to 0.6 times.

Some candidate explanations of a fast rate are excluded. The profiles run along [100], so crystal orientation cannot supply the 16-to-32-fold change the other axes would imply. Deep stalls of 10 minutes or more make the pyroxenes look slower than olivine. The cooling path slows the rate rather than speeding it. The Barth et al. laws describe dehydration of Fo 90 and Fo 80 olivine (their start-of-run and end-of-run versions differ by a factor of 5), and we keep them as sensitivity cases. On profile uncertainty, we keep the fixed 2023 uncertainties; a data-estimated uncertainty, with the calibration error carried in K, moves every rate by 8 % or less. The spot-to-spot uncertainty is rejected for both pyroxenes because they scatter two to four times more than it implies.
Two choices deserve a plain statement. First, the olivine K of Towbin et al. (2023) was built on the same SIMS calibration as the SR olivine data, so the central rate is on a consistent scale. The remaining calibration uncertainty is the 12 % offset of that calibration from the Withers et al. (2012) olivine line, which corresponds to a factor of 0.79 on the rate (0.125 against 0.155 MPa/s isothermal for the CO2/Nb start; about 0.113 for the MiMiC start). Second, the wet start rests on the intact interior opx cores of WHT1. Their deepest points reach 409 to 413 ppm, in equilibrium with 3.48 wt% melt H2O (opx-anchored K 117.7 ppm per wt%), within 2 % of the MiMiC start (3.549 wt%) and 3 % of the CO2/Nb start. The drier mixture start (SR-6, 2.72 wt% H2O) gives an olivine rate 12 % higher than the CO2/Nb start but a much worse joint fit (χ² 41, against 20 to 21 for the MiMiC and CO2/Nb starts, computed with the CO2 of the CO2/Nb start). Two grains plateau near 300 to 320 ppm instead, which we carry as an uncertainty in K or in the starting H2O (Chapter 9). Two further assumptions, a constant rate and the starting CO2, are tested in the next section.

title: 8  Stage II: final ascent in degassing magma
text:
8.5 Path shape and starting CO2
Does the rate depend on assuming a constant decompression rate, or on the starting CO2? Both are open questions. Bernard & Costa (2024) found that a constant-rate fit to a hot mafic magma that accelerated toward the surface overestimates its mean ascent rate at least twofold. Olivine-hosted inclusions in continental basanites carry 1.6 to 4.8 wt% CO2 (Buso et al. 2025) and up to 3.2 wt% (Hennig et al. 2026), well above our 1.41 wt% start.
Acceleration enters through the same warp as temperature. If the rate is \(v(P) = v_0\,a(P)\), the profile depends on time only through \((D_{ref}/v_0)\int r/a\,dP\). A fit on \(P_w = \int r/a\,dP\) therefore returns the deep rate \(v_0\) exactly. We let the rate ramp linearly from \(v_0\) at 60 or 200 MPa to 2, 5 or 10 times \(v_0\) at the surface. The profile fixes the near-surface rate, not the deep one (Table 8.4, Figure 8.4 a).

With 2 to 5 times acceleration: the mean rate over the last 60 MPa stays at 0.06 to 0.10 MPa/s and the surface rate at 0.10 to 0.12. The deep rate falls about in proportion, to 0.02 to 0.06 MPa/s.
With 10 times acceleration: the deep rate is bounded only from above at most path slopes, because a slow deep ascent keeps the olivine near equilibrium until the last stage.

Four analyses cannot resolve the shape of the path, so constant ascent remains the simplest fit. The headline rate is best read as the rate over the last ~60 MPa, where Ol-2 lost most of its water. If the magma accelerated, the mean rate from xenolith pickup could be 2 to 5 times lower. The same caveat holds for every published rate from a constant-rate fit, so the comparison in the next section stays on equal terms.
A higher starting CO2 makes the rate faster, not slower (Figure 8.4 b). The MiMiC start (8,529 ppm) gives rates about 10 % below the CO2/Nb start (14,100 ppm), the same direction. We ran two further MagmaSat paths from the CO2/Nb start (SR-1): 29,800 ppm (the ocean-island CO2/Nb of 505 times the lava Nb) and 36,000 ppm (the Buso et al. 2025 mean).

Degassing: they saturate at 1437 and 1613 MPa and lose half their H2O by 82 and 90 MPa, against 63 MPa for the CO2/Nb path (55 MPa for the MiMiC path).
Rates: olivine rises to 0.125 and 0.134 MPa/s (1.23 and 1.33 times) and the pyroxenes by 1.15 to 1.44 times.

The CO2-rich vapor strips H2O deeper, spreading the loss over a longer interval, so the same profile needs a faster ascent. All of these sit inside the 68 % ranges. The MiMiC start holds only the CO2 reconstructed from the richest inclusion, and the CO2/Nb start is the smallest CO2 that lies above every reconstructed inclusion, so the headline rate is, if anything, slightly low on this point (about 10 % for the CO2/Nb start). A melt with that much CO2 would already have been vapor-saturated at the 1.15 GPa pickup, and the equilibrium assumed there would need re-checking (Chapter 9). With the rate and its main assumptions in place, the next section sets it beside published ones.

(b) Rates against starting CO2 for Ol-2 and the WHT1 exterior opx and cpx. SR-wide P–T family.

title: 8  Stage II: final ascent in degassing magma
text:
8.6 SR among published eruptions
How fast is the SR ascent compared with eruptions studied with the same kind of model? The comparison uses only H2O diffusion with a degassing boundary (olivine phenocrysts, melt embayments and melt inclusions).
Figure 8.5 places the SR olivine rate among the published ones, and Table 8.5 gives the ratios. We compare each published rate with the olivine-only SR path rate of 0.093 MPa/s, not with the joint rate, because the published studies fit olivine alone. SR equals Seguam 1977 (ratio 0.93, 0.100 MPa/s; Newcombe et al. 2020). It is about one quarter of Fuego 1974 (0.23) and one fifth of Etna 3930 BP (0.20), which is the closest analog: primitive, Fo 90 olivine with CO2-rich inclusions. It is 1.9 times the published Kilauea Iki rate, and 3.1 to 10 times the Cerro Negro olivine rates (3.1 for 1995, 10 for 1992) of Newcombe et al. (2020) and 13 to 66 times the melt-inclusion rates of Barth et al. (2019).






Figure 8.5: SR decompressed as fast as Seguam 1977 and the slow end of the Kilauea fountains, about a quarter of the subplinian Fuego and Etna rates, and 3 to 11 times faster than Cerro Negro. The first four rows use the MiMiC start; the CO2/Nb start follows, and the sensitivity rows below it were run on the CO2/Nb start (isothermal).

The comparison puts SR on a fairer footing than before, though not an identical one. Every published rate in the set was modeled isothermally at the temperature of the study’s own inclusions or eruption (1030 to 1200 °C where stated). The SR path rate equals an isothermal fit at about 1150 °C, so the ratios compare SR’s best-temperature rate with each study’s single-temperature rate. The earlier isothermal SR rate, at 1200 °C, was hotter than every comparison except Kilauea Iki, and moving to the path lowers every ratio by about a third. A path treatment of the other studies would move their rates in the same direction: Chen et al. (2013) found that 50 K of extra cooling lowered their Vulcano rates from 0.003 to 0.021 to 0.002 to 0.015 MPa/s. Seguam 1977 from melt embayments (Mutch et al. 2024, 0.07 to 0.36 MPa/s) gives a ratio of 0.58 on the path (0.093 ÷ 0.16).
SR is a cinder cone, and it sits at the fast end of the cinder-cone and Strombolian range, with only Seguam 1977 matching it. Two readings fit this and the comparison alone cannot separate them. The SR magma may have risen faster than a typical cinder-cone magma: it is rich in CO2 and carried dense mantle xenoliths. Or the rate is biased high. The candidate biases have been narrowed. The olivine K and the SR data share one calibration, the pyroxenes fit the same history once their diffusivities are free, and the cooling path has already lowered the rate by about a third. The olivine K within its published range (factor 0.58 to 2.3) and the solubility model (0.55) remain the main levers, and neither brings SR down to the Cerro Negro range. CO2 content alone does not order the published rates either: CO2-rich Etna 3930 BP is fast like SR, while the CO2-rich Fogo and La Palma 2021 eruptions are slow by other methods and CO2-poor Fuego is fast. Eruption intensity tracks the rate better, as in Barth et al. (2019).
Published rates from H loss in mantle-xenolith olivine are not like-for-like. They fix the boundary at zero from the moment of entrainment, which makes them upper bounds on the equivalent rate; we return to them in Chapter 10. Having placed the rate among the other eruptions, the last question is how the degassing signal entered the xenolith at all.

section: 8.7 How the degassing signal entered the xenolith
text:
8.7 How the degassing signal entered the xenolith

Work in progress. The grain-boundary modeling in this section is still being revised. The current standard fits are the network fitted to each grain’s extrapolated rim (\(10^{-6.25}\) m²/s) and option B, one common start with a diffusivity per grain (\(10^{-5.75}\) m²/s); see the end of this section and appendix F (Section F.9). Outstanding: measured grain sizes and traverse geometry for every traverse (half or full widths, crossing traverses, elongate grains), a path-length factor for the distance to the xenolith exterior, the two interior grains at 40.5 and 40.8 mm, and the cpx coupling to the network.

How did a drop in melt water at the exterior of the xenolith reach its interior, and what does that say about the pathway? The opx grains across WHT1 act as sensors, as in the grain-boundary experiments of Demouchy et al. (2010).
The measured pattern is a gradient in how much water the opx rims have lost. The outermost spot of the exterior grain (0.5 mm from the xenolith exterior) holds 96 ppm, about 30 % of its 315 ppm core, while the rims of the interior grains (40.5 and 40.8 mm) approach their cores. If every grain sat directly in the degassing melt, all would show the same loss. They do not, so the boundary of each grain lags the melt, and the lag measures the transport through the xenolith.
We fit the WHT1 opx traverses (35 points) with each grain a slab with its own half-width and core, sitting in a 50 mm grain-boundary network whose diffusivity carries the melt’s fractional H2O drop inward; all grains share one opx diffusivity. The network uses an activation energy of 34 kJ/mol (Demouchy 2010) and opx 144 kJ/mol. We reran the fits at each joint-fit scenario, each at its own joint rate. Table 8.6 gives the result.

Four things follow. First, the scenario barely matters: the network diffusivity is \(10^{-5.4}\) to \(10^{-6.0}\) m²/s in every fit and is lowest only at 120 °C/GPa, where the slow rate gives the network more time. Second, the exterior grain is effectively unbuffered (g = 0.98), and the interior grains saw about half the melt’s drop (g 0.45 to 0.55) by the end of the ascent. Third, the 2023-style test, which treats each measured rim as the grain-boundary value, fails in every scenario (χ² 42 for 5 rims); the rims sit 19 to 45 µm inside each grain, so they lag the boundary. Fourth, the opx diffusivity of the nested fit (\(10^{-11.5}\) to \(10^{-11.6}\) m²/s) is lower than the joint-fit value for the exterior opx (−10.98); a coupled fit that lets the grains feed H back into the network gives −10.9 to −11.0, so the exchange data prefer a somewhat lower opx diffusivity than the exterior profile alone. The set-ups differ: the joint fit gives the exterior grain the melt as its boundary and a 423 ppm start, while the nested fit puts every grain behind the grain-boundary network and fits one opx diffusivity to all five traverses, including the heterogeneous interior grains (Chapter 9). We take the spread, about 0.6 log units, as the uncertainty of the opx diffusivity from these data.
A second way to read the same data avoids the lag inside the grains. Each grain’s own profile is extrapolated to its edge (a one-step diffusion profile with the core fixed), and the network is fitted to those four edge values. This gives \(10^{-6.25}\) m²/s (68 %: −6.35 to −6.15) at 0.100 MPa/s, with χ² 5.6 for 4 rims, and it is the fit shown in the Chapter 3 Figure 13 replica (Section F.9). The 0.5 mm grain extrapolates to about zero (−8 ± 42 ppm), so an edge that follows the melt fits it without buffering. A one-step profile treats the falling edge as constant, which biases this value low; the nested fit models the falling edge but places the 0.5 mm grain’s outermost point too high.
The nested set-up above starts each grain at its own measured core, which builds in an unchanged core and a different partition coefficient for each grain. The standard nested fit (option B) instead starts every grain at one common value with one opx partition coefficient and gives each grain its own opx diffusivity, for crystal anisotropy (scripts/decompression/gb_aniso_halfwidth.py). It fits all 35 points better (χ² 43.8 against 63.3) with a common start of 388 ppm (384–400; 411 ppm gives χ² 45.8) and a network diffusivity of \(10^{-5.75}\) m²/s (68 %: −5.81 to −5.68). The two exterior grains then agree with each other and with the joint fit (opx log D −11.1 and −11.0, against −10.98), and their plateaus below the start become core loss. The interior pair needs −11.8 and −10.4, a spread twice the largest published opx anisotropy (0.6 log units), so something local, most plausibly a melt vein near the 40.8 mm grain, acts there as well. Freeing each grain’s half-width (±25 % prior) changes χ² by less than 2. The two standard fits, extrapolated rims and option B, bracket the network diffusivity at \(10^{-6.25}\) to \(10^{-5.75}\) m²/s at the headline rate. The scenario table above uses the earlier measured-core set-up.
The fitted network diffusivity (\(10^{-5.4}\) to \(10^{-6.0}\) m²/s) is 1.6 to 5 times below the intrinsic olivine grain-boundary diffusivity of Demouchy et al. (2010) at 1200 °C (5 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s, \(10^{-5.3}\)). The coupled model, which lets the grains exchange with the network, gives the same network value (\(10^{-5.50}\) to \(10^{-5.75}\)) but cannot separate the diffusivity from the storage of water in the grains relative to the boundary, because the two trade off one for one at the same χ². The profiles constrain only the effective transport into the xenolith. A fixed common starting value fits worse than free per-grain starts: χ² 151 to 164 for 411 ppm and 101 to 108 for 321 ppm, against 57 to 58 when the starts are free. The preference for 321 ppm over 411 ppm comes from one heterogeneous interior traverse and is treated as a K or starting-H2O uncertainty (Chapter 9).

8.7.1 Which pathway carries the signal
Which physical pathway can carry a drop in water activity centimeters into a xenolith within about an hour? We compare four. The comparison separates two questions: how fast the signal travels, and how fast the water itself moves. Towbin & Plank (2026) give the physical constraints: 8 to 10 % interconnected vein and film melt in 2-D (about 20 vol% in 3-D), grain-boundary glass films extending 100 to 200 µm from the veins, vugs at 1 to 4 % of the rock, and host-like chemistry reaching only the outer centimeter.
Melt diffusion in the vein network (about 5 × 10⁻¹¹ to 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s) reaches only 0.4 to 0.9 mm in an hour, far short. Dry nanometer grain boundaries, weighted by how much water the grains hold, have an effective diffusivity of 10⁻¹³ to 2 × 10⁻¹² m²/s and reach 0.02 to 0.08 mm. Vapor in vugs and cracks (3 × 10⁻⁸ to 7 × 10⁻⁷ m²/s) reaches 11 to 51 mm. Only the intrinsic grain-boundary value of Demouchy et al. (2010) and the fitted network value (\(2\) to \(4 \times 10^{-6}\) m²/s) reach about 100 to 140 mm. The lengths come from the earlier mixture-start run over about an hour and scale as the square root of time; at the joint rate the interval is about 1.5 h, which lengthens them by about 20 %.
The profiles record signal relay, not mass transport. If the boundary network holds little water of its own, a drop in water activity travels at about the intrinsic grain-boundary diffusivity, and that is what the opx profiles show. Moving the water itself is a different matter. The vein melt holds 80 to 88 % of the xenolith’s H2O and the grains about 3 %. Transporting that mass centimeters along dry boundaries would need the storage-weighted value, which is 10⁻¹² m²/s or lower and far too slow. A closed-system mass balance suggests the vein melt is dry (about 0.09 wt% H2O, from a bulk-rock value of about 80 ppm and a bulk partition coefficient of 0.0034), a low-activity sink rather than a reservoir, though H2O in the vein glass has never been measured. The lag also argues against efficient in-place degassing of a water-rich vein melt, which would lower the activity everywhere at once with no lag from the exterior.
Figure 8.6 sets three candidate mechanisms against the measured rim-to-core ratios of the WHT1 opx grains. Melt-network diffusion alone, or melt pockets that keep their water, stop the signal within 1 to 3 mm and predict no depletion beyond the exterior grain. Grain-boundary transport at 2 to 5 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s matches three of the five traverses and under-predicts the exterior grain (0.5 mm) and the long interior traverse, whose cores are heterogeneous (310 to 409 ppm within one grain). The curves are on the CO2/Nb (wet) start with a constant 1200 °C: the melt and vapor diffusivity laws they need were not rerun on the path (they require temperature laws for melt and vapor diffusion), and the network diffusivity moves by 0.5 log units at most across the temperature scenarios, far less than the orders of magnitude that separate the mechanisms.






Figure 8.6: Only grain-boundary transport carries the melt’s water-activity drop to the xenolith interior: at 40.8 mm about 0.6 of the drop arrives by grain boundaries, none by the melt network. Columns: melt network, grain boundaries, hybrid. Rows: cartoon, water activity with distance, predicted against measured opx rim/core. CO2/Nb (wet) start, isothermal 1200 °C, 0.178 MPa/s (melt and vapor D have no temperature laws).



Demouchy et al. (2010) argued from Harrison’s regimes that hydrogen diffusion in grain boundaries cannot compete with lattice diffusion in coarse-grained rocks. Over the hour of H loss, the check gives a more qualified answer. Olivine (diffusion length 0.60 mm) is in the regime where its grains engage fully with the boundaries, and opx (\(10^{-11.2}\) m²/s, 0.15 mm) is in the regime where only its outer rim exchanges. During degassing the grains are sources, not sinks, but the released water still resists the fall in boundary activity. With dry nanometer boundaries holding melt-like water, the coupled fit would need a boundary diffusivity about 100 times Demouchy’s value, so the boundary phase decides: dry boundaries have the speed but not the storage, and micrometer melt films have the storage but not the speed. Fluid-wetted boundaries and cracks give both. Towbin & Plank (2026) report olivine pitting by fluid more than 150 µm from the veins, which supports that pathway. The conclusion is that a grain-boundary-type network, most plausibly fluid-wetted boundaries and cracks, carried the signal in WHT1, at a diffusivity consistent with the intrinsic value of Demouchy et al. (2010). Path-controlled transport predicts depletion set by each grain’s distance to a connected crack or vein, not to the exterior; mapping the vein and crack positions around the analyzed grains would test it.
All of these processes ran in the last tens of MPa of the ascent. The xenolith minerals must first have been in equilibrium with the host melt for the profiles to start from the right value, which is the subject of the next chapter (Chapter 9).
