title: 9  Stage I: ascent in water-undersaturated magma
text:
9.1 Do the olivine cores equal the phenocrysts, and was there time?
Stage I runs from xenolith pickup at about 1.15 GPa to the depth where the melt starts to lose water. The magma is H2O-undersaturated throughout (the MiMiC model melt saturates at 682 MPa and still holds 99 % of its H2O at 585 MPa), so H+ can move freely between melt and mineral. This chapter asks whether the xenolith minerals used that time to equilibrate with the host. Three tests bear on it: the olivine cores and the time the crystals spent in the melt, the starting levels of the intact orthopyroxene (opx) interiors, and the clinopyroxene (cpx) core water against the water in each magma.
Cores. The xenolith olivine cores in the GCB1 interior hold 4.3–8.7 ppm H2O (mean 6.89, n = 8) and those at the exterior 4.8–7.7 ppm (mean 5.95, n = 9). The scoria phenocryst cores hold 5.9–7.9 ppm (mean 6.77, n = 5). Interior and exterior xenolith groups do not differ statistically (Welch t = 1.38). Olivine inside the xenolith therefore carries the same water as olivine that grew in the host magma, which is what full equilibration with the host predicts. The check has limited power: n is small and the olivine cores have also lost water during Stage II (Chapter 8), so it shows that the cores share a history with the phenocrysts, not what that history was before degassing.
Time. Several clocks say there was ample time before the magma began to degas. Conduction heats a 65 mm radius xenolith in about 2 h. Hydrogen in the slowest phase, a 0.5 mm cpx, needs about 7 h at 1200 °C to reach a flat profile. The Fe–Mg profiles of olivine give residence times in the carrier of hours to weeks (Table 9.1), against a final ascent recorded by H of about 1.6 h from 585 MPa at 0.100 MPa/s.
Table 9.1 shows that even the shortest record, 0.15 d (3.6 h), exceeds the 1.6 h of H-recorded ascent by 2.2×. Ol-2 spent 18.4 d in the carrier, with its edge held at Fo 79.7, the rim value of its backscattered-electron (BSE) gray profile scaled to the EMPA Fo; the three starting profiles tested span 14–33 d (Section A.10). These are residence times in the carrier melt, so they bound the time available for exchange but not the length of Stage I itself.
Two pulses. The Fo data (Figure 9.1) show that the crystals in the scoria did not all come from one melt. The pit phenocryst rims reach Fo 83.3–85.8 (median 84.5), in equilibrium with the host lava (Fo 83.6–85.7). The roadside rims end 1–4 Fo units lower (Ol-2 at 80.7, ol6 at 81.5–82.6, ol23 at 83.0) and need a melt with 6.6–8.6 wt% MgO. Residence times differ in the same direction: 0.15–0.37 d for the roadside xenocrysts, 1.9–3.0 d for the pit xenocrysts. The roadside inclusions are also drier (1.96–2.80 against 2.41–3.55 wt% H2O) and lower in Cl/K2O. Two pulses of magma probably fed the two sampling sites. No measured inclusion records the final roadside melt, so the starting H of Ol-2 is not directly known (Chapter 11).
The olivine says the minerals had time and the same history as the host. Whether they ended at the host’s water level depends on what the opx interiors hold.

title: 9  Stage I: ascent in water-undersaturated magma
section: 9.2 What do the opx interiors say about the starting water?
text:
9.2 What do the opx interiors say about the starting water?
The ascent-rate fits need a starting level for the grains before water loss began. The best anchor is the interior of the large WHT1 opx, which sat 40 mm inside the xenolith, far from the degassing exterior.
The picture is less tidy than “intact cores at 411 ppm” (Figure 9.2). Two of the five traverses, the exterior opx at 0.5 mm and the interior opx-2 at 40.8 mm, flatten near 300–320 ppm. Only the two deepest single points reach 409–413 ppm. The interior opx-1 rises steadily to 413 ppm with no plateau. For the exterior grain, a flat 315–321 ppm center is no evidence of the start: the joint fit reproduces it as loss from a 423 ppm start that reached the middle of this small grain (χ² 0.9). The interior opx-2 grain is different. A 300 ppm shelf with a 409 ppm point behind it cannot come from one starting value diffusing inward, so this grain was probably zoned before the final water loss.






Figure 9.2: Two WHT1 opx grains flatten near 300–320 ppm, and only the two deepest points reach 409–413 ppm. H2O in opx against distance from the rim for the five traverses, by grain and depth in the xenolith. Lines: opx-anchored K times melt H2O for the wet CO2/Nb start (423 ppm; 418 ppm for the MiMiC start), the mixture start (320 ppm) and the two intact cores (411 ppm).



Two fits disagree about which level to use. The rate model, fitted to the exterior opx and cpx, fits with the MiMiC melt (3.549 wt% H2O): joint χ² 20.0 isothermal, against 41.5 for the mixture start (SR-6, 2.72 wt% H2O; computed with the CO2/Nb start). The exchange model, fitted to all five WHT1 traverses with one common start, prefers the lower level: χ² 104 at 321 ppm against 154 at 411 ppm. Nearly all of that difference is one traverse, interior opx-2 profile 1 (χ² 64 against 106). When each traverse may choose its own start, the values scatter from 215 ppm to the 600 ppm bound, so no single common start fits every interior grain.
The two levels can be read in two ways, and the data do not choose between them.

K uncertainty. A 300–320 ppm start in the MiMiC melt (3.549 wt%) needs K of 85–90 ppm per wt% (84–89 for the CO2/Nb start, 3.59 wt%), an opx/melt D of about 0.009 and 25 % below the Novella-anchored value (117.7). The experimental range is 0.009 to about 0.019 (K about 90–190), so both levels lie inside it.
Starting-H2O uncertainty. With K = 117.7 ppm per wt%, the plateaus equal the mixture batch (2.72 wt%) and the deepest points the wet batch (3.49 wt%, against 3.549 wt% in the MiMiC melt and 3.59 wt% in the CO2/Nb start). Both are measured Sullivan Ranch melts.

We keep the MiMiC start for the rate because the exterior grains that record the rate fit it best. The interior grains started heterogeneous, which fits grains that last equilibrated with different batches. Either reading removes a single clean “intact core” anchor.
The opx cores thus point to a melt of 2.7–3.5 wt% H2O, in the range of the Sullivan Ranch inclusions. The cpx cores add a test across volcanoes.

section: 9.3 Do cpx cores track the water in their magmas?
text:
9.3 Do cpx cores track the water in their magmas?
Cpx is the slowest phase, so it is the strictest test. We compared the cpx core water with that of the melt at each volcano, using the cpx/melt partition coefficient D from the experiments of O’Leary et al. (2010). Equation 10 of that paper was refit to 28 experiments recalibrated onto the SIMS scale of Towbin et al. (2023), with tetrahedral Al excluding the Cr-Tschermak component (residual σ 0.21 in ln D).
Wetter magmas carry wetter xenolith NAMs, with one outlier. Cima, the driest magma (1.29 wt% H2O), holds the driest cpx (113 ppm). The Sullivan Ranch cores (341–451 ppm) sit in the wettest magma. Vulcan’s Throne cores (421 ppm) are as wet as Sullivan Ranch’s in a drier magma (2.29 wt%), so the ordering holds only partly (Figure 9.3).
The cores hold 1.2–2.6× what the experiments predict (Table 9.2). Against the maximum melt H2O of each volcano, Cima and WHT1 sit within 1σ, WHT06_1 is 1.7σ off, GCB1 2.5σ and Vulcan’s Throne 2.7σ. The cpx diffusion fits agree independently: started from the experiment-based K, they pull K up by 1.6–1.9×, which means a cpx/melt D of about 0.011–0.016. The opx row differs because its K is anchored to the opx cores, so a ratio near 1 is by construction.

Figure 9.3: Wetter magmas carry wetter xenolith cpx, but the cores hold 1.2–2.6× the water the recalibrated experiments predict, and Vulcan’s Throne cpx are as wet as Sullivan Ranch’s in a drier melt. (a) Mean cpx core H2O against host-melt H2O (horizontal bars: best-estimate melt H2O range; vertical: 1 SD of the cores), grey band the experimental prediction. For Vulcan’s Throne and Cima the horizontal bar runs up to the soft maximum from literature H2O/Ce (265) times Ce: 3.23 and 1.64 wt%. The nearly undegassed Sullivan Ranch inclusions (H2O/Ce 149–416) cover that literature range. A single ratio times whole-rock Ce does not predict Sullivan Ranch itself (2.25 against 3.55 wt%), because its H2O varies with Cl, not Ce. (b) Observed against predicted cpx/melt D (1 sigma), with the 1:1 line.



Four readings could explain the excess, and none has been tested. The cores may have kept some pre-entrainment water, though the clocks above argue against it. The melt may have held more water than the inclusions record. The cpx/melt D may be higher at these conditions, for example rising as melt H2O falls, as for olivine. Or the recalibration of the experiments may be off (the Cr-rich Hauri set has no recalibrated values, and Aubaud 2004 sits 1.5× above the others). The Cr-Tschermak argument does not rescue the match: removing the Cr-Tschermak Al shifts D by 3–7 %, and explaining Vulcan’s Throne against Cima would need a Cr coefficient of −42 per apfu, outside what the experiments allow.
This revises a conclusion of the earlier chapter, which called the agreement quantitative. That comparison set recalibrated xenolith D against uncorrected experimental D. On a common scale the qualitative result stands (drier magma, drier cpx) and the quantitative one weakens. The pyroxene diffusion fits already use the opx-anchored cpx K, which agrees with what the cpx data choose, so the rate does not depend on the experimental D. Cpx cores therefore track the water of their host magma in order and within a factor of 1.2–2.6 in amount.
Together the three tests say that the minerals had time, and that their water follows the host melt. What that leaves of the mantle’s water is the question of the next chapter.

crumbs: 9  Stage I: ascent in water-undersaturated magma

title: 10  Stage 0 and implications
text:
10.1 What survives of the mantle water?
Stage 0 is the lithospheric source: the water the xenolith minerals held in the mantle before the host magma picked them up. This chapter asks what of it survives in the Sullivan Ranch (SR) xenoliths, what that means for xenolith water studies elsewhere, and what the xenoliths are still good for.
Nothing measurable in these xenoliths. The chain of evidence has three links, each from the preceding chapters.
Two limits apply. The cpx excess shows that partitioning is not settled, so the agreement is not quantitative. A cpx that retained mantle water would look the same as one that equilibrated with a wetter melt than the inclusions record, and no test here separates the two. We cannot exclude, but find no evidence for, a surviving mantle component in the cpx cores. The conclusion that nothing survives therefore rests mainly on the timescale argument, with the partitioning as a consistency check that is weaker than first reported.
The conclusion holds for hot alkali basalt carried in a cinder cone: a magma near 1200 °C with weeks between pickup and eruption. It says nothing about cooler or faster carriers.
Stage 0 leaves nothing to read, so the useful question becomes what this means for other studies.

title: 10  Stage 0 and implications
text:
Time was ample. The crystals sat in the carrier melt for at least 3.6 h (shortest Fe–Mg record, 0.15 d) and up to 18 d (Ol-2), against about 7 h for a 0.5 mm cpx to reach a flat profile at 1200 °C and about 1.6 h for the final ascent recorded by H (Table 9.1).
The minerals track the host. Olivine cores in the xenolith match the phenocrysts (6.89 and 5.95 ppm against 6.77 ppm). The opx interiors sit at 300–413 ppm, in equilibrium with a melt of 2.7–3.5 wt% H2O when the opx-anchored K is used, which is the range of the SR inclusions (Section 9.2). The cpx are wetter in wetter magma and hold 1.2–2.6× what the recalibrated experiments predict (Section 9.3).
The signal that did enter is the host’s. Every grain lost water at its rim during final ascent (Chapter 8), and the interior grains see the drop with a lag that a fast transport network explains (Chapter 8).

title: 10  Stage 0 and implications
section: 10.2 What does this mean for xenolith water studies?
text:
10.2 What does this mean for xenolith water studies?
Hot alkali basalts of cinder cones are the worst case for fidelity. Diffusion of H+ through crystals, grain boundaries and melt is fast near 1200 °C, and the ascent from the mantle takes days to weeks. The minerals are reset. A study of xenoliths from such a host needs a measured host-magma water content, a P–T path and a degassing path before its mineral water can be read as mantle water. Cooler and faster hosts such as kimberlites, nephelinites and melilitites may preserve mantle water, but that needs constraints on their ascent rates, temperatures and water contents.
Published xenolith-NAM rates are upper bounds and not like-for-like. Several studies convert H loss from xenolith olivine into an ascent velocity. They fit a fixed boundary: zero H outside the crystal from entrainment onward, or a constant rim. They divide the full source depth (35–70 km) by the H-loss time. Our model, like those of Newcombe et al. (2020) and Barth et al. (2019), uses a boundary that follows the degassing melt, so H loss is confined to the shallow part of the path. When most of the loss is shallow, a velocity computed over the whole depth overstates the true constant velocity. Peslier et al. (2015) show the sensitivity inside one study: its rates rise 1.8× when the assumed start of loss moves from 1 to 1.8 GPa. The published rates also scale linearly with the diffusivity assumed, and Peslier & Luhr (2006) use a value that is the mean of two experimental values a factor of 10 apart.
Table 10.1 lists the published rates beside the SR olivine rate on the P–T path. The ratios run from 0.25 to 72: SR is slower than three studies, equal to Meerfelder Maar and faster than four. Because the published values are upper bounds, a ratio below 1 would shrink and one above 1 would grow if the studies were rerun with a degassing boundary, so SR is, if anything, faster relative to them than the table shows.

A consequence for earlier work is specific. Demouchy et al. (2006) derived ascent from 60–70 km in hours from Pali-Aike olivine. If the Pali-Aike host carried water comparable to SR, the H-loss time would belong to the final 6 km and the implied velocity would fall by an order of magnitude. The water content of that host is unknown, so this remains a hypothesis to test, but it shows why the host water and degassing path are the first things to measure.
Reset xenolith water is a loss for mantle studies. It is a gain for a different question, treated next.

title: 10  Stage 0 and implications
section: 10.3 What are xenoliths good for instead?
text:
10.3 What are xenoliths good for instead?
They are timekeepers of the final ascent. The same grains that lost their mantle water recorded the speed of the magma that carried them. On the P–T path the joint fit of olivine Ol-2 and the WHT1 exterior opx and cpx gives 0.100 MPa/s (0.050–0.200 over the slope envelope of 46–120 °C/GPa), 0.63× the isothermal 1200 °C joint rate of 0.158. At 0.10 MPa/s the magma rises about 3.6 m/s, and the stretch where the melt loses half its H2O (below about 55 MPa) takes minutes. The CO2/Nb start, the second scenario, gives 0.112 MPa/s.
Two clocks together give the whole path. Fe–Mg profiles in olivine give weeks of residence in the carrier, and the H profiles give a final ascent of about an hour and a half from 585 MPa. The thesis chapter described the contrast as acceleration from about 0.002 MPa/s through most of the path to about 0.2 MPa/s in the upper crust. The updated rate is 0.100 MPa/s on the cooling path, so the contrast is about 50× rather than 100×. The deep rate is the thesis estimate (at least a week from 1.15 GPa) and was not remeasured; the Fe–Mg times are residence times in the carrier, not ascent times.
The xenolith also records how the signal moved. The exterior grain saw the melt boundary directly (g 0.98), and the interior grains saw about half the drop. The effective network diffusivity, 10^-6.25 to 10^-5.75 m²/s at the headline rate from the two standard fits, is 3–9× below the olivine grain-boundary value of Demouchy (2010) (5 × 10^-6 m²/s). Xenoliths can thus constrain transport inside a magma body as well as its speed.
The SR rate sits with Seguam 1977 (0.93×) and at about 0.2× Fuego 1974 and Etna 3930 BP. It is 3.1–10× faster than Cerro Negro. These comparisons use the olivine-only path rate of 0.093 MPa/s against each study’s rate at its own temperature, not refits of the published studies (Chapter 8).
Sources: summary workbook sheets Literature_Rates (block B), Other_Timescales and Magma_Models; Towbin et al. thesis chapter (Stage 0 and implications); docs/LITERATURE_ASCENT_RATES_2026-10-21.md for the boundary-condition argument.

title: 11  Open questions for co-authors
text:
11.1 Questions for Terry
Which choices could still change a finding, and which of them need an expert call rather than more analysis? The list below is short on purpose: it names only the items that could move a conclusion.
CO2/Nb as the second scenario for the starting melt. The primary start is the published MiMiC melt (3.549 wt% H2O, 8,529 ppm CO2, saturation 682 MPa). The inclusions lost CO2 before trapping, so that path starts partly degassed: bubble-reconstructed CO2 reaches only 9,079 ppm, and the inclusions saturate at 129–574 MPa, far shallower than xenolith pickup (1.15 GPa). The second scenario adds CO2 back as CO2/Nb times the Nb of the lava (59 ppm). With the depleted-mantle ratio of 239 (Saal et al. 2002) the start has 14,100 ppm CO2 and saturates at 922 MPa, close to pickup. With the ocean-island ratio of 505 ± 168 (Rosenthal et al. 2015) it has 29,800 ppm and saturates at 1,438 MPa, deeper than pickup. The rate depends on the choice by about 10 % (joint fit 0.100 MPa/s for the MiMiC start against 0.112 for CO2/Nb; Ol-2 isothermal 0.143 against 0.155), but the depth story does not survive without it. Terry is asked to judge whether the CO2/Nb scenario should stay as a second scenario or be dropped.

title: 11  Open questions for co-authors
text:
Which ratio? Is 239 or 505 the better reference for an enriched alkaline basalt?
Which Nb? Should each inclusion use its own LA-ICP-MS Nb instead of the lava value? With each inclusion’s Nb and a ratio of 239, undegassed CO2 is 11,400–20,500 ppm and saturation 670–900 MPa (Iacono-Marziano), against 190–450 MPa as measured.
Whether to correct at all. Is the correction worth making for a summary of this kind? CO2/Ba gave 3–7× more CO2 and was rejected, because the SR Ba/Nb (11.5–16.5) lies far above that of the reference pairs.

title: 11  Open questions for co-authors
text:
11.2 Model questions
Cpx partitioning. The cores hold 1.2–2.6× the water that the recalibrated experiments predict (Table 9.2). Is the cause pre-entrainment water, a wetter melt than the inclusions record, a higher D at these conditions, or the recalibration of the experiments? No test separates them yet.
Opx starting levels. The opx plateaus at 300–320 ppm and the deepest points at 409–413 ppm can be read as K uncertainty (K of 84–89 against the anchored 117.7 ppm per wt%) or as different starting H2O (the mixture and the wetter batch). The rate model fits with the MiMiC (or CO2/Nb) start and the exchange model prefers the lower one (Section 9.2). Is there independent evidence to choose a K?
Transport laws on the P–T path. The two tables on transport mechanisms (mechanism curves and transport estimates) still run on the earlier mixture path. They need temperature laws for melt and vapor transport before they can be moved to the P–T path, and the grain-boundary activation energy (34 kJ/mol) is taken from one experimental study. Should they then use the single median slope (82.8 °C/GPa) or the full slope family?
Path shape. The olivine profile fixes the rate over the last ~60 MPa but not the deep rate (Section 8.5). - Constraint: a magma that accelerated 2 to 5 times toward the surface would have a mean ascent rate from pickup 2 to 5 times below the headline. - Test: only a phase that loses water deeper could tell, such as the cpx rims, which form deeper than the opx and olivine rims, or an inclusion record of the CO2 loss. Is any such test worth making?

title: 11  Open questions for co-authors
text:
11.3 Data questions still open

Matched exterior pyroxenes. The modeled exterior opx (0.5 mm) and cpx (7.5 mm) come from different exteriors of WHT1, so their rates are not a like-for-like pair (Section 8.3). Should the pyroxene fits be repeated with a matched pair: Exterior-2 opx-1 and cpx-1 (both 7.5 mm), or Exterior-1 opx-2 and cpx-2 (0.5 and 1.45 mm)?
Cpx calibration standard. A NanoSIMS standard row named “opx_ignore” sits in the cpx fit. If it is not intended, every cpx concentration changes slightly, and so does the partitioning test.
Experimental scale factor. The thesis workbook’s “Kd-corr” is exactly 0.75 times the published-scale D. Does that come from the SIMS-scale factor of the cpx experiments (mean 0.769)?
Roadside final melt. No inclusion or matrix glass samples the melt that set the roadside rims, so the starting H of Ol-2 is unmeasured. A drier carrier would make the rate faster (the 2.72 wt% start gives 1.12×).
Rounded cpx line and scaling. Fifteen cpx analyses were typed with a rounded calibration line (0.2–1.4 ppm low), and two (T1-218 and T1-219) were rescaled for SiO2. Small, but should they stay as in the SIMS dataset (Supplement Table S2)?

Sources: summary workbook sheets Magma_Models and Other_Timescales; the working list of supplement questions; the older uncertainty chapter.

title: Appendix A — Diffusion model and fits
text:
A.1 The decompression model
This appendix holds the method detail behind the decompression rates: the diffusion model and its Bayesian fit, the data and priors, the choice of a fixed uncertainty per profile, the warped-pressure treatment of a falling temperature, the diffusivity laws and partition coefficients, the edge and stall tests, and the supporting tables for the Fe–Mg residence of Ol-2 and for the xenolith exchange fits. The rates themselves are in Chapter 8. The primary start for every fit is the published MiMiC melt (3.549 wt% H2O, 8,529 ppm CO2; saturation 682 MPa); the CO2/Nb start (SR-1, 3.59 wt% H2O, 14,100 ppm CO2) is the second scenario. Tables below that were computed before the change of primary start are marked as CO2/Nb-start tables.
The model is the one used in the 2023 MATLAB fits, ported to Python (~/Projects/H2O_Diffusion_NAM/decompression/) and reproduced to ≤ 1e-14 relative. Pressure falls linearly, \(P(t) = P_0 - v t\), over a total time \(t_\mathrm{tot} = (P_0 - P_f)/v\). The crystal is a one-dimensional slab of half-width L with a no-flux center and a rim held in equilibrium with the degassing melt:
\[
\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = D\,\frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial x^2},\qquad
\left.\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0} = 0,\qquad
C(L,t) = K\,H\big(P(t)\big),\qquad
C(x,0) = K\,H(P_0)
\tag{A.1}\]
C is H2O in the crystal (ppm), H(P) the melt H2O along the degassing path (wt%, Appendix C) and K the mineral/melt partition coefficient in ppm per wt% (10⁴ times the dimensionless D of Appendix C). The crystal starts in equilibrium with the melt at P0. That start is justified by the P–T history: from xenolith pickup (about 1.15 GPa) to saturation (923 MPa) the melt H2O is constant, and between saturation and P0 (about 585 MPa) the SR-1 melt loses only 4 % of its H2O, so H in the xenolith minerals and in the phenocryst is free to equilibrate and nothing is lost before P0. The model is a one-dimensional slab; Mutch et al. (2024) show that 1-D fits can underestimate H loss by about 30 % for 3-D crystals.
Exact property 1: one dimensionless time. Rescaling \(\xi = x/L\) and \(s = t/t_\mathrm{tot}\) turns Equation A.1 into \(\partial C/\partial s = \tau\,\partial^2 C/\partial \xi^2\) with the rim value \(K\,H(P_0 - (P_0 - P_f)s)\), where
\[
\tau = \frac{D\,t_\mathrm{tot}}{L^2} = \frac{D\,(P_0 - P_f)}{L^2\,v}.
\tag{A.2}\]
The data constrain τ, not D and v separately, so \(v = D(T)(P_0 - P_f)/(\tau L^2)\), and a change of diffusion law rescales the fitted rate exactly (\(v_\mathrm{new} = v_\mathrm{old}\,D_\mathrm{new}/D_\mathrm{old}\)). The discrete scheme is invariant too (≤ 3e-16 relative on all ten 2023 cases). L is not a pure rescaling, because the measured distances are fixed in µm.
Exact property 2: K only scales the profile. The problem is linear and homogeneous, and the initial and rim values are proportional to K, so \(C(\cdot\,; K) = K\,C(\cdot\,; 1)\). With data \(h_i \pm s_i\) and model \(K g_i(\tau, P_0, P_f)\), a Gaussian prior \(K \sim N(\mu_K, s_K^2)\) integrates out in closed form. With \(a = \sum g_i^2/s_i^2 + 1/s_K^2\) and \(b = \sum h_i g_i/s_i^2 + \mu_K/s_K^2\),
\[
\log p(h \mid \tau, P_0, P_f) = -\tfrac12\Big[\sum_i \frac{h_i^2}{s_i^2} + \frac{\mu_K^2}{s_K^2} - \frac{b^2}{a}\Big]
- \tfrac12\log\!\big(a\,s_K^2\big) - \sum_i \log\!\big(\sqrt{2\pi}\,s_i\big).
\tag{A.3}\]
The closed form matches numerical integration over K to 1e-8. It needs negligible prior mass at K < 0, so K priors wider than about 16 % (1σ) are run as several fits instead.

title: Appendix A — Diffusion model and fits
section: A.2 Grid posterior, data and priors
text:
A.2 Grid posterior, data and priors
Because the dimensionless profile \(G(\xi; \tau, P_0, P_f)\) does not depend on the data, it is tabulated once per case and degassing path: 400 values of log τ (from the explicit solver’s floor to 2.5), nodes at the ends of the P0 and Pf prior ranges interpolated onto 15 × 6 cells, and a spatial grid twice as fine as the 2023 one. The priors sit on the physical parameters, and the posterior
\[
p(\log v, \log D, P_0, P_f \mid h) \propto
\exp \ell\big(\log D + \log(P_0 - P_f) - 2\log L - \log v,\ P_0,\ P_f\big)\; p(\log v)\,p(\log D)\,p(P_0)\,p(P_f)
\tag{A.4}\]
is evaluated on a grid of 350 log v cells (0.02 dex) × 21 log D nodes × the P0 × Pf cells, with the K-marginal log-likelihood ℓ (Equation A.3) interpolated in log τ. It is exact to grid resolution, with no MCMC noise, and replaces the 2023 Monte Carlo of optimizer solutions, whose spread mixed the D prior, the data noise and optimizer stopping error. Validation: table entries equal direct forward runs; log v quantiles move by less than 0.01 dex when the τ and v grids are doubled; and on synthetic profiles drawn from the priors the 68 % and 95 % intervals contain the truth at their nominal rates. Ascent speed is \(u = v/(\rho g)\) with ρ = 2800 kg/m³.

title: Appendix A — Diffusion model and fits
section: A.4 Variable temperature: the warped pressure
text:
A.4 Variable temperature: the warped pressure
On the P–T path (Chapter 3) the temperature falls, \(T(P) = 1330\ \mathrm{°C} - s\,(2.26\ \mathrm{GPa} - P)\), so D falls with pressure: \(D(t) = D_\mathrm{ref}\,r(T(P(t)))\) with \(r = \exp[-(E_a/R)(1/T - 1/T_\mathrm{ref})]\) and \(T_\mathrm{ref}\) = 1200 °C.
Why it is exact. With reduced time \(\theta = \int_0^t D\,dt'/L^2\) the diffusion equation becomes \(\partial C/\partial\theta = \partial^2 C/\partial\xi^2\) again, and only the rim value as a function of θ changes. For continuous ascent, \(dP = -v\,dt\), so
\[
\int D\,dt = \frac{D_\mathrm{ref}}{v}\int r\big(T(P)\big)\,dP,
\qquad
P_w(P) = \int_0^{P} r\big(T(P')\big)\,dP'.
\tag{A.5}\]
Reduced time is linear in the warped pressure \(P_w\) with the constant rate \(D_\mathrm{ref}/v\). The constant-D problem with rim value \(K\,H(P(P_w))\), run on the warped pressure (with the path and the P0 and Pf priors mapped through \(P_w\)), is the variable-temperature problem, and its fitted v is the true ascent rate. No new solver or approximation is involved (scripts/decompression/fit_pt_path.py).
Activation energies. Each phase uses the mean Ea of its two bracket laws: olivine 130 kJ/mol (Ferriss, one law); opx 144 kJ/mol (Carpenter 127 and 161); cpx 115 kJ/mol (the 100 and 130 kJ ends of the 2023 cpx bracket).
Slopes and families. Fits are run at slopes of 30–150 °C/GPa in 15 °C/GPa steps. The scatter of the start (N(1330, 15) °C, N(2.26, 0.10) GPa) is carried as an effective slope with the same temperature at 30 MPa. Each family’s rate is a mixture of the per-slope posteriors (lognormal from the median and 68 % range) over that family’s slope distribution.
Controls.

With r = 1 the warped fits reproduce the isothermal fits of the MiMiC start exactly: 0.143 (olivine), 0.256 (opx) and 0.728 (cpx) MPa/s (opx-anchored K) [CHECK: the exact-reproduction control was run on the CO2/Nb start, 0.155, 0.290 and 0.874].
A direct implicit solver with D(T(P(t))) agrees with the warped model to 0.0215 wt% at slopes of 30, 90 and 150 °C/GPa. The two solvers differ by the same amount at 1200 °C, so the warp itself adds no error.
Running the pyroxenes with the ends of their Ea brackets moves their rates by ±10 % (opx 0.109–0.134, cpx 0.397–0.477 MPa/s at 105 °C/GPa).
The degassing path stays the 1200 °C MagmaSat path; evaluating solubility along the P–T path changes the rates by ≤ 3 % (Appendix C).

All three phases slow by nearly the same factor on the path (0.63–0.69 across the SR-wide envelope), because their Ea (115–144 kJ/mol) are similar. The path changes the rates but not the disagreement between phases.
Accelerating ascent. For a rate \(v(P) = v_0\,a(P)\), \(dt = -dP/(v_0 a)\), so \(\int D\,dt = (D_\mathrm{ref}/v_0)\int r/a\,dP\). The same fit on \(P_w = \int_0^P r/a\,dP'\) is exact, and its fitted rate is \(v_0\), the rate above the ramp. - Shapes: \(a = 1\) above \(P_a\) and \(a = F - (F-1)P/P_a\) below it, with F = 2, 5, 10 and \(P_a\) = 60, 200 MPa. - Prior: the lower edge of the rate prior is moved down by \(\log_{10}F\). - Derived rates: the mean rate over an interval (\(\Delta P / \int dP/(v_0 a)\)) and the surface rate (\(F v_0\)) are fixed multiples of \(v_0\), so the slope-family mixture is taken on \(v_0\) and scaled. - Control: the constant shape reproduces the path fits to 6 × 10⁻¹⁷ MPa/s. - Scope: Ol-2 only, K = 9.
Higher starting CO2. Closed-system MagmaSat paths from the CO2/Nb start, SR-1 (same melt, H2O, Fe3+/FeT and 1200 °C) at 29,800 and 36,000 ppm CO2. They are fitted for Ol-2 (K = 9) and the WHT1 exterior opx and cpx (all K strategies) over the same slope grid. The 14,100 ppm path reproduces the path fits to 2 × 10⁻¹⁶ MPa/s, and the primary path’s hash is unchanged by the rebuild.
Code. scripts/decompression/fit_path_variants.py {accel|co2} and plot_path_variants.py; outputs in results/decompression/path_variants/.

A.5 Olivine diffusivity
Why [100]. Ol-2 is a host-scoria phenocryst (Fo 87.8 core to 84.3 rim, TiO2 140–210 ppm), inside the Ferriss calibration range (Fo 85–95) at the core and at its boundary toward the Barth et al. (2019) range (Fo 75–85) at the rim. Its SIMS traverse runs along [100]. Orientation matters: along [010] or [001] the Ferriss laws are 0.03–0.06 times the [100] value, and a profile perpendicular to a random face would average about 0.36 times [100]. Because the profile is along [100], orientation does not explain the fast rate.
Laws (Table A.4). 55 olivine H diffusivity laws from 18 sources are transcribed in data/olivine_h_diffusivity/laws.csv, and the pyroxene laws in data/pyroxene_h_diffusivity/laws.csv and at_1200C.csv. title: Appendix A — Diffusion model and fits
text:
A.6 Olivine/melt partitioning






Figure A.1: Olivine/melt partitioning of total H2O falls as melt H2O rises if olivine H follows melt OH (Peterson et al.), while the Towbin et al. (2023) value is constant; the two agree near 1 wt% melt H2O. Points: Peterson et al. experiments (10–200 MPa, 1000–1220 °C; filled, the six H2O-saturated runs with olivine grown in the run). Blue curve and band: D_OH = 0.0011 ± 0.0002 times the OH fraction from VolatileCalc-basalt speciation. Dashed: Peterson’s power law. Grey band: Towbin et al. (2023), 0.0009 ± 0.0003. Orange: the 2023 model prior. Light-blue column: melt H2O in equilibrium with the GCB1 olivine rims. Coefficients are dimensionless (times 10⁴ for ppm per wt%).



Two published treatments are compared (Figure A.1, Table A.5):

Towbin et al. (2023): constant K = 9 ppm per wt% (0.0009 ± 0.0003). It combines earlier experiments recalculated onto the revised opx-standard SIMS calibration (KBH-1 = 202 ppm) with inclusion–olivine pairs, and it resolves no dependence on melt H2O or pressure below 2 GPa. Its ±33 % range is run as three fits (K = 6, 9, 12), each with a 15 % prior. The 2023 MATLAB prior, N(9, 0.5), was six times narrower than the paper; the deposited Fig. 11 caption value of 0.009 is a typo for 0.0009.
Peterson et al. (Am Min 111): olivine H follows melt OH, with D_OH = 0.0011 ± 0.0002 and the OH fraction from VolatileCalc-basalt speciation (scripts/model_choices/speciation.py, which reproduces their 25 glasses to ≤ 0.005 wt%). The effective K is then 6.5 at 2.72 wt% melt H2O, 9.5 at 0.9 wt% and about 11 below 0.3 wt%. It enters the fit as an effective path, K0 × OH(H), with K0 = D_OH ~ N(11, 1.8) integrated out as before.

The Peterson power law is only a sensitivity bound. Peterson et al. print \(C_\mathrm{ol} = 10.52\,C_\mathrm{melt}^{0.52}\) once, “for ease of adaptation of existing code”, fitted to six H2O-saturated grown-olivine runs spanning 2.0–4.8 wt% melt H2O; an unweighted refit of those six gives a coefficient of 10.2 ± 2.3 and an exponent of 0.54 ± 0.17. D_OH and the power law agree above about 1.5 wt% (17.6 against 17.7 ppm at 2.72 wt%) but diverge below it: the power law’s effective K rises without limit as melt H2O approaches zero (19 at 0.3 wt%, 32 at 0.1 wt%), while D_OH levels off near 11. On the wet path the power law gives 0.083 MPa/s extrapolated and 0.104 when K is held constant (12.1) below the lowest experiment (0.75 wt%). About a third of the halving comes from that extrapolation; the rest comes from 0.75–2 wt%, constrained only by two undersaturated runs about 200 °C hotter. The olivine rate is most sensitive to K in the last 1–2 wt% of degassing, where the rim forms and partitioning is least constrained. D_OH is therefore the Peterson case, and the power law is a bound on low-H2O partitioning, not a preferred model.

title: Appendix A — Diffusion model and fits
text:
A.7 Pyroxene diffusivities and partitioning
K strategies. The xenolith pyroxenes did not grow from the host melt: H that diffuses into them decorates inherited defects, so experimental K are a prior, not a law. The evidence that they re-equilibrated with the host is that all three phases scale with the magma between volcanoes and that cpx/opx in the same xenolith (0.96–1.38) matches the experimental mineral/mineral ratio (Aubaud et al. 2004: 1.4 ± 0.3). Each pyroxene profile is therefore fitted three ways (Table A.5): core/start (the boundary starts at the measured core, the 2023 approach), opx-anchored (Novella × 0.93 for opx, the opx value times the cpx/opx core ratio for cpx), and experiment-based. The 0.93 factor puts Novella’s opx on the revised opx SIMS scale of the xenolith data (Towbin et al. 2023). The 2023 priors (opx N(90, 5), cpx N(120, 5)) have no literature source and are not used.
The intact cores fix the start. The deepest core points of the interior WHT1 grains (opx 413.5 and 408.5 ppm, mean 411; cpx 375.6 and 404.4, mean 390) are taken as the cores that kept the host-melt value (scripts/decompression/fit_wet_primary.py). With them, core/start K for opx is about 118, equal to the opx-anchored 117.7, and the opx core implies 3.48 wt% melt H2O, within 2 % of the MiMiC start (3.549) and 3 % of the CO2/Nb start (3.59). Only the two deepest points reach these levels (409–413 ppm), while two grains flatten near 300–320 ppm; the main text treats that as an uncertainty in K or in the starting H2O (Chapter 9). The exterior opx (0.5 mm from the xenolith exterior) is effectively unbuffered, and the exterior cpx (7.5 mm in) is moderately buffered, which changes its implied D by less than 0.1 log units.
Pyroxene D from the olivine rate. The 2023 approach fits olivine first and then asks what pyroxene D its rate implies. Property 1 makes this exact: a pyroxene profile fixes \(\tau_\mathrm{px}\), so a known v gives \(\log D = \log\tau + 2\log L + \log v - \log(P_0 - P_f)\). Two versions were run (pyroxene_d_from_olivine.py, pyroxene_d_on_path.py, joint_d_fit.py):

Method A combines each pyroxene’s τ posterior (flat log D prior, 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻⁸ m²/s) with independent draws of the olivine v posterior. Check: the implied opx-exterior D equals the bracket midpoint × v_ol/v_opx (10−11.08 against 10−11.09).
Method B fits one history to Ol-2, the WHT1 exterior opx and cpx together, with free log D for opx and cpx and olivine fixed at Ferriss [100]. Run on the P–T path with joint_d_fit.py --slope S, each phase diffuses on its own warped clock (same Ea as above). The warped-time solver agrees with the warped-pressure model within 0.21–0.55 % of the initial value, the same as at 1200 °C (0.24–0.57 %).

With the MiMiC start one continuous ascent fits all three phases, and on the P–T path the joint fit gives 0.100 MPa/s at 82.8 °C/GPa (χ² 20.6 for 20 points; CO2/Nb start 0.112 MPa/s, χ² 19.5). The opx sits on Carpenter 2003 [100] (San Carlos enstatite, the slow axis), and the cpx on the slow natural Cr-diopside laws (Ingrin 1995; Hercule & Ingrin 1999 uptake) and the Ferriss 2016 3540 cm⁻¹ band, about 2.5 times below Ingrin 1995. The faster opx laws (Demers-Roberge 2021, on Al-poor enstatite with 0.11 wt% Al2O3) would need olivine rates about 7–20 times faster. The SR opx carries 3.3–3.9 wt% Al2O3 and the cpx is Cr-diopside, so the slow Al- and Cr-bearing laws are the plausible ones. Figure A.2 compares the implied diffusivities with published laws. The cpx upper bound of the 2023 bracket (\(10^{-6.71}\exp(-100\ \mathrm{kJ}/RT)\)) was the thesis estimate for a cpx with 0.07 tetrahedral Al, extrapolated from Ferriss et al. (2016), who publish laws for Kunlun diopside but no equation for the Al dependence; its prefactor matches their 3540 cm⁻¹ band law and its activation energy their bulk-H law. The implied cpx D lies just below the bracket’s lower end.






Figure A.2: Few published pyroxene laws match the H diffusivity that the SR exterior profiles need to agree with the olivine rate: 1 of 9 opx laws (Carpenter 2003 [100]) and 3 of 16 cpx laws fall in the 95 % interval. Implied log10 D at 1200 °C for WHT1 opx (a) and cpx (b) from the olivine posterior (circle, median; thick bar, 68 %; thin bar, 95 %; one row per olivine K option, opx-anchored pyroxene K), and the range of the joint fit across stall durations (diamond), against published laws (open circles). Shaded: the 2023 model bracket. These fits use the mixture start (2.72 wt%) at 1200 °C; the wet start and the P–T path shift the implied D by 0.15 log units or less (Table A.6).

title: Appendix A — Diffusion model and fits
text:
A.8 Olivine edge tests
Measured olivine edges often stay above zero, in natural phenocrysts and in dehydration experiments (Newcombe, Ferriss, Barth), which suggests a diffusion–reaction process near the rim. Two treatments were tested on Ol-2.
The final-pressure prior (scripts/decompression/olivine_pf_sensitivity.py). In the NAM model the edge value at the end of ascent is K × H(Pf), the treatment of Barth et al. (2024). The 2023 prior capped Pf at 5 bar and the posterior pressed against it (3.3 bar). Widening it to 0–20, 0–50 and 0–200 bar moves the fitted Pf to 10–17 bar (edge boundary 1.8–2.4 ppm) and the rate within 0.155–0.164 MPa/s with K = 9 (0.146–0.160 with Peterson D_OH). Given room, the data prefer a quench pressure of about 1–2 MPa, comparable to the about 2 MPa used by Newcombe’s group. Ol-2 is insensitive because its outermost analysis is 23 µm in (4.4 ppm), so the profile does not sample the true edge.
A two-population model after Barth et al. (2023) (scripts/decompression/olivine_barth_effects.py). Mobile H diffuses with the Barth start-of-run [100] law (4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s at 1200 °C) and is in equilibrium with the melt at the edge; trapped H is immobile and relaxes toward r × mobile at a rate k; the total equilibrium partitioning is K = 9. In the fast-exchange limit this is one species with \(D_m/(1 + r)\); with slow exchange the mobile H drains while the trapped H stays, giving a high edge and an apparent D that falls with time, Barth’s “apparent locking of H+ at the crystal edge”. v is fitted for trapped fractions 0.2–0.67 and k = 10⁻⁵–1 s⁻¹ on the wet path (P0 585 MPa, Pf 1 MPa, σ 0.25 ppm), with Crank–Nicolson for mobile H and an exact exponential exchange step. Controls: with no trapping the model reproduces the single-D fit, and with r = 1 and fast exchange it equals a single species with D/2 to < 0.01 ppm.






Figure A.3: Barth-type edge locking cannot fit Ol-2: only fast exchange of trapped H (k ≳ 0.1 s⁻¹) reproduces the profile, and then the model reduces to an effective diffusivity. (a) Best-fit Ol-2 decompression rate and (b) misfit (χ², 4 points) against the exchange rate of trapped H, for trapped fractions 0.2–0.67, in a two-population model whose mobile H diffuses with the Barth et al. (2023) start-of-run [100] law (wet SR-1 MagmaSat path, 1200 °C, K = 9). Dashed: single D, Ferriss [100] (0.150 MPa/s, χ² 5.7). Dotted: single D, Barth start-of-run (0.62 MPa/s). Rates of 0.003 MPa/s at k ≤ 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ are the bottom of the search grid and belong to rejected fits.



Figure A.3 shows the result. Fast exchange (k = 1 s⁻¹) fits as well as a single D (χ² 5.7–5.8) at 0.21–0.50 MPa/s; slow exchange (k ≤ 0.01 s⁻¹, which gives Barth-like edges at 11–53 % of the initial) fits badly (χ² 21–7000). Slow edge locking is inconsistent with Ol-2, which kept only about 25 % of its equilibrium start, because an immobile pool of ≥ 20 % cannot leave. Barth’s effects therefore collapse to an effective D, and the bulk laws for natural olivine (Ferriss, Barth end of run) give 0.13–0.15 MPa/s, inside the diffusivity-law range. The test assumes Ol-2 started in equilibrium with the deep melt; its early-grown Fo 88 core supports that. The pyroxenes were not tested, since Barth’s effects are documented for olivine only.

title: Appendix A — Diffusion model and fits
text:
A.9 Stall and post-eruptive tests
Could a stall, rather than the pyroxene diffusivities, explain why the three minerals give different single-ascent rates? Two tests were run with the 2023 pyroxene diffusivities fixed and the mixture start (2.72 wt%) at 1200 °C (scripts/decompression/scenarios.py, stall_fit.py). They are summarized here because the joint fit with free pyroxene D supersedes them: with the 2023 diffusivities a short stall halved the misfit, but the joint fit with free pyroxene D needs no stall.

Forward scenarios. Each phase was modeled with its own radius, D (bracket midpoint) and K under continuous ascent, a stall (ascent to Ps, a closed hold at H(Ps), final ascent) or a post-eruptive hold at the surface value, then refitted with the continuous model with only v free. The Crank–Nicolson solver matches the NAM forward model to 0.5 %. Stalls at 15–30 MPa push the wrong way (the olivine resets during the stall, while the pyroxenes carry it, so the pyroxenes look slower than olivine). Only a hold at the very end (a stall shallower than about 5 MPa, or time at the surface before quench) makes olivine slower than the pyroxenes. History cannot separate opx from cpx, because their bracket-midpoint D are nearly equal. Core reset times (\(L^2/D\)) are 3.6 min (olivine), 14 min (cpx) and 34 min (opx), so the survival of the Ol-2 profile limits any post-eruptive hold to well under the olivine reset time.
Joint stall fit with the 2023 D. One history was fit to all three phases with the stall pressure set by the flat GCB1 xenolith-olivine plateau (Ol-6, 7.2–7.8 ppm, giving 16.6 MPa). A pause under 2 min after a fast deep ascent halved the misfit on every olivine calibration, stalls of 10 min or more fit worse than none, and even the best fits were poor (χ² 153–317 for 20 points, mostly cpx); the best final ascent stayed at 0.07–0.3 MPa/s.

With the MiMiC start and free pyroxene D a stall is not needed at the central slope (Table A.7 shows the CO2/Nb-start stall scan). Continuous ascent gives χ² 20.0 isothermally against 20.2 for the best 5-minute stall, and 1–3 min stalls fit worse than continuous ascent. title: Appendix A — Diffusion model and fits
text:
A.10 Fe–Mg residence of Ol-2
Ol-2’s Fe–Mg profile gives the time it sat in the final carrier melt, which is much longer than the H ascent (about 1.6 h from 585 MPa at 0.1 MPa/s), so its H re-equilibrated before ascent, the equilibrium start assumed at P0. The EMPA traverse runs along the same line as the SIMS H traverse, which is along [100], so the [100] fits are the result and the [001] fits (the fastest Fe–Mg axis) are a lower bound on time (Figure A.5, Table A.8).
The headline fit holds the crystal edge at Fo 79.7. A backscattered-electron (BSE) gray profile of Ol-2, taken near the EMPA line, scales linearly to the EMPA Fo (Fo = 98.2 − 0.183 × gray, RMS 0.17 Fo, 24 points) and reaches Fo 79.7 at the outermost clean pixel, 1.6 µm from the edge, 1 Fo below the outermost EMPA point. With the edge held, the two-step start gives 18.4 d (15.7–21.3) and fits the outer 10 µm; the time barely changes from the edge-free fit (18.3 d). The BSE profile also shows the 40–90 µm shoulder that every model misses, so the misfit there is in the grain, not the analyses (Figure A.4).

title: Appendix B — Melt-inclusion methods
text:
B.1 Three MiMiC versions
This appendix holds the melt-inclusion method detail behind Chapter 6 and the starting melt of the ascent models: the three MiMiC versions and their error budget, the bubble equation of state, which MiMiC run sets the P–T path, the LA-ICP-MS and host checks, the olivine-overlap correction, GC2_ol4, and the CO2 basis of the start (CO2/Nb against CO2/Ba).
MiMiC (Rasmussen et al. 2020) corrects each inclusion for post-entrapment crystallization (PEC) and adds back the CO2 in the vapor bubble with a bubble-growth model. Three versions are compared:
The published construction has two errors that partly cancel. Its Redlich–Kwong CO2 volume is 6–8 % too small (against Span–Wagner), which gives too much CO2. Treating the CO2 mole fraction as a volume fraction ignores the H2O in the vapor, which gives too little CO2 for H2O-rich vapor. For SR (vapor CO2 mole fraction 0.35–0.52 in the key inclusions) the second error is larger, so the modified version adds bubble CO2. Table B.1 gives the values for the 12 SR inclusions used in the P–T path fits.
Across whole eruptions the median change in bubble-corrected CO2 from v2 to v3 is +3.4 % for SR (13 inclusions with a bubble), −0.9 % for Vulcan’s Throne and −1.1 % for Cima. The maximum-H2O inclusion (Ol23) and the maximum bubble-CO2 inclusion (GC2_ol7) are the same in every version.
The H2O–CO2 pattern of the three volcanoes does not change with the version (Chapter 6). Across 39 inclusions the Duan & Zhang correction changes bubble-corrected CO2 by −2.8 to +14.8 %, and 34 stay within ±5 %.

B.2 Monte Carlo uncertainty and error budget

title: Appendix B — Melt-inclusion methods
text:
B.3 Bubble equation of state
Nine bubble-fluid models were compared on all 40 inclusions (scripts/bubble_eos/): published Redlich–Kwong; Span–Wagner CO2; ideal mixing with IAPWS-95 H2O; modified Redlich–Kwong and Duan & Zhang (2006) H2O–CO2 mixtures; and fixed CO2 mole fractions 0.8, 0.9 and 1. Duan & Zhang at the equilibrium vapor composition was adopted, with the modified Redlich–Kwong result (2–5 % more CO2 for H2O-rich vapor) as the spread. The vapor composition still comes from VolatileCalc with ideal mixing. Raman CO2 densities of the bubbles would test the choice. The observed-volume CO2 is not used where the measured bubble exceeds 3 times MiMiC’s modeled shrinkage bubble (co-entrapped vapor); only Ol23 (3.4 against 2.08 vol%) passes.

Why the headline rate does not depend on the version. The primary rate on the P–T path starts from the published MiMiC melt (3.549 wt% H2O, 8,529 ppm CO2), the row “2026 recipe, 3.549 / 8,529” of Table B.4, so the version question applies to it directly: the modified code changes the rate by 1.4 % or less. The second scenario, SR-1, has H2O (3.59 wt%) equal to Ol23’s H2O (3.55 wt%, identical in the two code versions) plus a 0.04 wt% back-calculated loss to CO2-rich vapor before trapping; its CO2 (14,100 ppm) is CO2/Nb 239 times the lava Nb, not a MiMiC value. The vapor-loss term was computed with the modified bubble CO2 and not rerun with the original code [CHECK: vapor-loss term with the original code].
Three things are robust to the choice: every inclusion H2O value (and so the H2O–Cl batch structure and the maximum-H2O inclusion), the identity of the highest-CO2 inclusion (GC2_ol7) with the conclusion that every inclusion trapped a CO2-degassed melt, and the decompression rates (≤ 1.4 %). The 2026 inputs (recalibrated pit NanoSIMS volatiles, corrected Ol36_2 CO2) differ from the 2023 ones, and those changes move the inclusion values more than the code does.

title: Appendix B — Melt-inclusion methods
section: B.7 CO2 of the start: CO2/Nb or CO2/Ba
text:
B.7 CO2 of the start: CO2/Nb or CO2/Ba
The tables show the published MiMiC CO2 first, as the primary start, and the CO2/Nb correction as the second scenario. Bubble-reconstructed CO2 (modified MiMiC) reaches 9,079 ppm (GC2_ol7), and the SR inclusions saturate at 129–574 MPa (Pvbg), shallower than xenolith pickup (1.15 GPa).
The CO2/Nb estimate. Undegassed CO2 is CO2/Nb times Nb. With the depleted-mantle ratio 239 (Saal et al. 2002) and the lava’s Nb (59 ppm), CO2 is 14,100 ppm, the start of the second scenario. The ocean-island-basalt ratio, 505 ± 168 (Rosenthal et al. 2015), doubles it (29,800 ppm). Sources: data/la_sims_2026/endmember_co2.csv, scripts/endmember_co2.py.

Every inclusion sits below the undegassed CO2 at either ratio. On the basis of each inclusion’s own LA-ICP-MS Nb and CO2/Nb 239, the trapped melts had already lost 46–91 % of their CO2 (retained 9–54 %), but at most 0.21 wt% H2O. On the lava-Nb basis the best inclusion (9,079 ppm) has lost 36 % of 14,100 ppm. This appendix quotes the per-inclusion basis unless it says otherwise.
With each inclusion’s own Nb and CO2/Nb 239, the undegassed CO2 is 11,400–20,500 ppm and the undegassed saturation pressure (Iacono-Marziano) 670–900 MPa, against 190–450 MPa as measured.
CO2/Ba was tried and rejected: it gives 3–7 times more CO2, because the SR Ba/Nb (11.5–16.5) is far above that of the reference pairs.
The rate depends on it by about 10 %. The as-trapped MiMiC start (8,529 ppm) gives 0.143 against 0.155 MPa/s (isothermal) for CO2/Nb 239, and the joint fit 0.100 against 0.112 on the path, since CO2 sets where degassing starts and the H loss happens below about 60 MPa.
It matters for the depth story. With CO2/Nb 239 the start saturates at 922 MPa (MagmaSat; the MiMiC start 682 MPa), close to xenolith pickup; with 505 it saturates at 1.44 GPa, deeper than pickup.

Open questions for co-authors are whether 239 or 505 is the right reference for an enriched alkaline basalt, whether a per-inclusion Nb is better than the lava Nb, and whether the correction is worth making at all (Chapter 11).

title: Appendix B — Melt-inclusion methods
text:
B.8 LA-ICP-MS against SIMS
LA-ICP-MS traces exist for 7 SR inclusions (GC2_ol3, ol5, ol8, Ol19, Ol35, Ol36_1, Ol36_2), and none for GC2_ol6, GC2_ol7, Ol11, Ol23, Ol21, Olxx or any Cima or Vulcan’s Throne inclusion. Figure B.2 summarizes the cross-checks.






Figure B.2: Laser ablation finds host olivine in the ablated volume of 6 of the 7 SR inclusions, SIMS S and Cl disagree with EMPA, and the two high-MgO inclusions sit on an olivine-admixture line instead of at Fe–Mg equilibrium. (A) LA-ICP-MS against EMPA content of major oxides for the 7 SR inclusions with LA data (symbol = oxide, color = inclusion; open symbols = the oxide used as the LA internal standard); points above the 1:1 line mean olivine in the LA spot. (B) SIMS against EMPA S and Cl for SR and Cima inclusions (solid line 1:1, dotted 0.5:1). (C) Apparent olivine–melt Fe–Mg Kd against EMPA MgO for all inclusions, with the equilibrium band 0.30 ± 0.03 and the mixing line of GC2 scoria glass plus 0–30 % Fo85 olivine. Data: data/la_sims_2026/.




Olivine in the laser spot. LA finds host olivine in the ablated volume of 6 of 7 inclusions (1–54 %; Ol19 52 %). Incompatible traces are unaffected to about 2 %; the LA calibration itself is good to about ±10–25 %.
SIMS against EMPA S and Cl. For the pit inclusions (NanoSIMS) SIMS S is 1.22–1.64 times EMPA, except Ol36_2 (0.89), and Cl is 0.88–1.33 times. For the roadside GC2 inclusions the comparison is circular, because their SIMS values were corrected with EMPA S, Cl and P (Section B.9). For Cima, SIMS S is 0.53–1.06 times and Cl 0.37–0.77 times EMPA, consistent with SIMS spots that hit olivine.
GC2_ol6 and Cima 06b_a are olivine-admixed analyses. Their apparent Kd (0.547 and 0.441) is far above equilibrium (0.30 ± 0.03). Melting of the measured Fo 85–86 wall cannot do that; a mechanical mix of glass and host olivine can. MiMiC’s 11–18 % post-entrapment “melting” for these two removes an artifact, so GC2_ol6 is excluded. Cima 06b_a (equilibrium Fo 88.9 against host Fo 85.9, so MiMiC removes olivine and scales the volatiles up) and Cima 12_a (no host Fo in the input, so its temperatures and PEC are not meaningful) stay in the inclusion tables, flagged, with these reasons.
Trace ratios. CO2/Nb (21–130 with the Duan & Zhang bubble) is 0.05–0.58 times the depleted-mantle 239, so CO2 was degassed before trapping and no bubble correction over-corrects. F/Nd (19.4–24.2 in four inclusions, against about 21 for oceanic basalts) independently confirms SIMS F.
H2O/Ce. H2O varies less than Ce (log-log slope 0.23), but Cl and S fall off against Ce almost as much, so at most about 20 % of the H2O decoupling looks like H loss, and 3.55 wt% is not clearly a minimum.
A supplement table error. In all six AZ18 rows of the melt-vein supplement table S9, the MiMiC oxide columns belong to other inclusions (reversed order); the H2O and bubble-CO2 columns are correct. It needs fixing before publication.

title: Appendix B — Melt-inclusion methods
section: B.9 The olivine-overlap correction (GC2 and Vulcan’s Throne)
text:
B.9 The olivine-overlap correction (GC2 and Vulcan’s Throne)
The SIMS volatiles of the roadside AZ09-GCB inclusions and of Vulcan’s Throne in the deposited tables are not raw. They carry the Plank-lab correction for SIMS overlap with host olivine, which scales each analysis using S, P and Cl; it is not the post-entrapment crystallization correction. Evidence: the 2023 overlap-corrected source table is titled “these have been corrected for overlap with olivine, using S, P and Cl”, with the raw EMPA SO2, P2O5 and Cl beside the corrected SIMS values, and the same values appear in the melt-vein supplement. Two Vulcan’s Throne inclusions marked “hit ol” (no EMPA) are uncorrected, but their Cl is scaled by 1.239 like every row, so Cl was also recalibrated. The MiMiC PEC correction was tested and ruled out (7–16 %, two negative, unrelated). The exact per-inclusion factor could not be reproduced from the EMPA and SIMS ratios (mean, geometric mean, least squares), so the formula is the Plank lab’s [CHECK: ask Terry Plank whether the supplement must state the formula]. No value changed; footnotes mark the affected rows.

title: Appendix B — Melt-inclusion methods
section: B.10 GC2_ol4 has no measured volatiles
text:
B.10 GC2_ol4 has no measured volatiles
The 2023 overlap-corrected source table lists EMPA for GC2_ol4 mi 02 but no SIMS volatiles, and Plank & Forsyth (2016) has no row for it. The 2023 MiMiC input gives GC2_ol4 S 1530, Cl 500, H2O 2.39 and CO2 3136, which are GC2_ol3’s values exactly, copied across in 2023. The deposited Table 3 row for GC2_ol4 (H2O 2.16 wt%, CO2 2840 ppm after PEC) is therefore GC2_ol3’s volatiles on GC2_ol4’s composition. The later melt-vein input leaves them blank, correctly. GC2_ol4 stays out of the inclusion tables, and the 2023 edition of the supplement keeps the deposited row with a footnote.

title: Appendix B — Melt-inclusion methods
section: B.11 Host candidates and the lava-versus-inclusion liquid line
text:
B.11 Host candidates and the lava-versus-inclusion liquid line
The degassing paths use the AZ09-UK01 lava as the starting composition. The checks ask whether a better host exists and whether the lava is the parent of the trapped melts (Figure B.3).






Figure B.3: The crystallization-corrected SR inclusions sit off the olivine control line through the AZ09-UK01 lava in 6 of 10 variables (FeOT, MnO, CaO, Na2O, P2O5 and CaO/Al2O3; panels outlined), so the lava is not their parent by olivine alone. Oxides and CaO/Al2O3 against MgO (wt%, anhydrous, all Fe as FeOT) for the 13 SR inclusions as measured (open grey circles) and after the MiMiC crystallization correction (filled blue), and after crystallization plus Fe-loss correction (open blue); GC2_ol6 as triangles. Large square: lava AZ09-UK01; large diamond: scoria AZ09-GCB; lines: olivine control lines; green lines: MELTS fractional crystallization of the lava at 180 MPa (3.4 wt% H2O) and 400 MPa; small grey points: Uinkaret Plateau whole rocks (Plank & Forsyth 2016 Table S6, n = 39).




AZ09-UK01 is the best SR host candidate. Among the Plank & Forsyth (2016) magmas it scores best in every variant (combined score 4.97 against 7.02 for the AZ09-GCB scoria; 4.77 against 6.96 with the Fe-loss set). No alternative improves on the 2023 choice.
The lava is a liquid but not the parent of the trapped melts. It is in equilibrium with Fo 85.3, the median GC2 olivine, with no sign of accumulated olivine or mantle debris. No sensible crystallization of up to four phases, and no forward MELTS path, links it to the inclusions within 2σ on every oxide: the inclusions are higher in CaO/Al2O3 and P2O5 (by about 20 %) and lower in TiO2, ratios that olivine cannot change.
Fe loss explains most of the apparent gap. With the recommended initial FeO (11.59–11.73 wt% on the scoria olivine control line; Ol23 11.69, GC2_ol7 11.62), the main inclusion mean comes within 2σ of the lava in 7 of 10 oxides.
Effect on the start. For the 2026 recipe, AZ09-UK01 saturates at 6815–6824 bar; moving it along olivine control to the inclusion mean changes this by −0.4 to +2.2 %, and AZ09-GCB would add 11.6–17.3 %.

title: Appendix B — Melt-inclusion methods
text:
B.13 Methods and code
MiMiC runs. MiMiC (Rasmussen et al. 2020), upstream commit 346a3dd, is vendored unchanged in scripts/mimic/vendor/. Settings: vb_cor = 1, fe_fixed = 0, fe_cor = 1, kd_model = 0 (Toplis 2005), H2O_diff = 0; 1000 Monte Carlo draws; numpy seed 1. Point values are the unperturbed first draw and do not depend on the seed. The SR Fe3+/FeT is blank in the input, so MiMiC uses a fixed 0.2 without resampling; Cima (0.17) and Vulcan’s Throne (0.23) are given and resampled. Cima and Vulcan’s Throne have no measured uncertainties, so their errors were assumed from the median SR relative errors (data/mimic_2026/assumed_relative_errors.csv). A shift of the last error columns in the SR input file was tested by realigning them: point values are identical and 1σ changes by ≤ 12 %.

Control. The 2023 input (42 rows) run through the vendored code with the 2023 settings reproduces the 2023 output and Table 3 to max |difference| 0.005.
Speed. scripts/mimic/run_mimic.py run --fast --jit --workers 12 is 46 times faster (SR, 1000 draws: 24 s); with the original global seed it is byte-identical to the original code.
Modified version. scripts/bubble_eos/run_production.py patches a generated copy of the driver (never the vendored file) at the two bubble CO2 sites. With the patch off, the output is bit-identical to version 2 at 1 and 1000 draws. Each output carries a .run.json with the settings, seed, equation of state and file hashes.
Error budget. scripts/mimic_methods/methods.py switches off one perturbation source at a time with aligned random streams (300 paired draws).
PEC and Fe loss. MiMiC adds or removes equilibrium olivine until the melt is in Fe–Mg equilibrium with the measured host Fo. The production runs apply no Fe-loss correction. Two code issues were found and left unchanged in the vendored file: the Fe–Mg exchange step uses a factor 2.298 where a 1:1 molar exchange needs 1.7825, and the resampled initial FeO is never used in the Monte Carlo.
LA-ICP-MS versus SIMS. scripts/la_sims/ reads the melt-vein supplement workbook; olivine in the LA spot is estimated with a two-component mixing model in which the internal-standard oxide sits in the glass only. The test suite has 16 passing tests.
Rates by MiMiC version. scripts/decompression/fit_mimic_compare.py reuses the fitting code and K strategies and changes only the degassing path (310 posterior rows).
Original volatiles and host checks. scripts/original_volatiles/ (VESIcal 1.2.12; MagmaSat in the ENKI ThermoEngine container, with a control reproducing the cached 6814.82 bar), scripts/starting_melt/ (matching the 2023 path onsets across 399 candidates), scripts/host_candidates/ and scripts/lld/ (least-squares mass balance; rhyolite-MELTS 1.2.0 with MnO removed from the bulk, which restores Fe–Mg olivine in this ThermoEngine build). The working logs are indexed in Appendix E.

title: Appendix C — Degassing models
text:
C.1 Accuracy on melts like ours
This appendix holds the evidence for the choice of solubility model, the comparison of the four models, the starting-melt paths with their refreshed saturation pressures, the temperature test of the solubility models, and the way the equilibrium boundary meets the measured xenolith rims. The main text uses the result: one closed-system MagmaSat path from the published MiMiC start, with the CO2/Nb start (SR-1) as the second scenario (Chapter 8).
Every degassing path is computed from one starting melt (H2O, CO2, composition, temperature) at its saturation pressure down to 1 bar. Four mixed H2O–CO2 solubility models were compared (Figure C.1, Table C.1): MagmaSat, Iacono-Marziano and Dixon (all through VESIcal) and MafiCH (Allison et al. 2022). Shishkina was assessed but not run on the path grid.
Hughes & Saper (2026 preprint) evaluate the VESIcal models on 770 vapor-saturated experimental glasses. Their per-experiment outputs were recomputed for an analog window around the SR melts (volatile-free SiO2 43–49 wt%, Na2O + K2O 3.5–6.8 wt%, T < 1350 °C): 111 experiments on 8 compositions, reaching 620 MPa at most. Recomputing their own Table 2 from these files reproduces the paper (for example MagmaSat −1.6 / 54.7 against their −2 / 55), which checks the scorer.
A model that overpredicts saturation pressure for a given melt H2O underpredicts H2O solubility at a given pressure. For nearly pure H2O vapor, dissolved H2O goes roughly as the square root of pressure, so MagmaSat’s +27 % bias below 200 MPa corresponds to about −11 % in dissolved H2O. That is the direction and roughly the size of MagmaSat’s low late-stage H2O (0.67 against 0.92 wt% for Iacono-Marziano at 10 MPa on SR-1). Below 200 MPa the analog test therefore favors Iacono-Marziano, but on 14 MagmaSat and 33 Iacono-Marziano experiments only. The saturation-pressure uncertainty to carry is about ±20 % (1σ) for both on analogs, and above about 0.6 GPa no model has been tested on compositions like ours.

title: Appendix C — Degassing models
section: C.2 Choice of model and comparison
text:
C.2 Choice of model and comparison

MagmaSat is primary. It is the most accurate model at 200–620 MPa on analogs, Hughes & Saper’s best model for alkali-rich melts (−9 / 22 %), the only model with no pressure ceiling in its calibration (our starts saturate at 0.43–1.7 GPa), it uses Fe3+/FeT, and it reproduces the 2023 path exactly.
Iacono-Marziano is a sensitivity case, mainly below about 200 MPa. It is the most accurate model there on analogs. The two are never blended, because a switch or weighted blend at about 200 MPa would put a kink into dH2O/dP that the diffusion boundary would fit as a change in degassing rate. Only the isothermal olivine rate exists on this path (0.086 MPa/s against 0.155 on MagmaSat, a factor of 0.55); no P–T path or pyroxene fits were run on it [CHECK: run the Iacono-Marziano path through the P–T and joint fits if it is to be called co-primary].
Dixon (VolatileCalc) is a sensitivity case. It reads +27 % high on analogs, it is outside its pressure calibration for every start, and its CO2 solubility depends directly on the SiO2 passed to it.
MafiCH is a check. It is not in VESIcal and was not evaluated by Hughes & Saper. It is calibrated at 1200–1250 °C only, with a composition-independent H2O law (Lesne et al. 2011). Its CO2 calibration includes a basanite and a leucitite, and the SR inclusions sit inside its cation-fraction ranges (Ol23 at the edge in Si). On the 3.55 wt% / 9079 ppm reference start it saturates at 736 MPa and holds 2.07 wt% H2O at 50 MPa and 0.84 at 10 MPa, between MagmaSat and Iacono-Marziano.
Shishkina is not recommended (precision 56 % on analogs, calibrated to 500 MPa only).







Figure C.2: The models disagree on saturation pressure and on melt H2O at 50 MPa, but all lose most of the H2O below about 100 MPa. Closed-system paths at 1200 °C from one reference start per volcano. Left column: SR lava AZ09-UK01, 3.55 wt% H2O and 9079 ppm CO2 (saturation 524–736 MPa across the four models; grey: the 2023 MagmaSat path, 3.36 wt% and 8529 ppm). Middle: Cima whole rock MO10-16, 1.33 wt% and 4196 ppm. Right: Vulcan’s Throne whole rocks AZ09-UK02 (solid) and AZ94 (dashed), 2.29 wt% and 5898 ppm. Bottom row: below 200 MPa. MafiCH (SR only) stops where about 10 ppm CO2 remains (about 4 MPa, closed). Each volcano uses only its own composition.



The four models are compared on one reference start per volcano in Figure C.2. Every SR path loses most of its H2O late. Half of the starting H2O is still dissolved down to 15–88 MPa, and the last 100 MPa removes 51–96 % of it. At 10 MPa every SR path holds 0.67–1.08 wt% H2O whatever its start: MagmaSat 0.67–0.74, Dixon 0.76–0.94, Iacono-Marziano 0.84–1.08. One factor at a time around the 3.55 wt% / 9079 ppm reference (Iacono-Marziano, closed), melt H2O at 10 MPa moves by 0.25 wt% with the model, 0.08 with CO2, 0.07 between closed and open, 0.05 with starting H2O (2.6–4.5 wt%), 0.02 with composition and less than 0.001 between 1166 and 1200 °C.
Open against closed. Open-system degassing keeps the melt 0.18–0.35 wt% wetter at 50 MPa but only 0.05–0.07 wt% wetter at 10 MPa, so the fits use closed-system paths, which also make the temperature correction simple.

title: Appendix C — Degassing models
section: C.3 Starting melts and saturation pressures
text:
C.3 Starting melts and saturation pressures
All SR paths use the AZ09-UK01 lava as analyzed (Plank & Forsyth 2016 Table S5; Fe3+/FeT 0.167). It is in equilibrium with Fo 85.3 against a host median of Fo 85.6 and carries no accumulated olivine, cpx or mantle debris. The inclusion mean (corrected for post-entrapment crystallization and Fe loss) is the composition bracket; it lowers the MagmaSat saturation pressure by about 10 % and changes melt H2O at 10 MPa by 0.02 wt% or less. The primary start is the published MiMiC melt (3.549 wt% H2O, 8,529 ppm CO2). The other starts carry 14,100 ppm CO2, the depleted-mantle CO2/Nb (239) times the melt Nb (59 ppm), the smallest undegassed CO2 that still lies above every reconstructed SR inclusion (Section B.7). Table C.2 gives their saturation pressures and Table C.3 the shape of each path. The starts span the H2O batches of Chapter 6: the published MiMiC melt (primary), SR-1 (wet end, CO2/Nb second scenario), SR-7 (wet end with Fe-loss correction), SR-6 (mixture of batches, the sensitivity case), SR-4 (dry batch) and Ol23 as trapped. The wet start was adopted because the intact interior WHT1 opx cores (about 411 ppm) with the opx-anchored partition coefficient are in equilibrium with 3.48 wt% melt H2O, within 2 % of the MiMiC start and 3 % of SR-1 (Section A.7).

title: Appendix C — Degassing models
text:
C.7 Methods and code
Code and outputs. scripts/degassing_paths/ writes data/degassing_paths_2026/ (cases.csv, paths.parquet, metrics.csv, xenolith_boundary.csv, figures/). The isotherms and the T-consistent refit are scripts/decompression/solubility_t.py. The starting-melt saturation pressures come from scripts/original_volatiles/start_psat.py and the MagmaSat runs from queue_magmasat.py, run_magmasat.sh and scripts/original_volatiles/collect_magmasat.py (control: 6814.82 bar reproduced). Tests: tests/test_degassing_paths.py.
Compositions. Anhydrous Plank & Forsyth (2016) analyses with FeO and Fe2O3 split at each vent’s Fe3+/FeT, normalized to 100 − H2O − CO2 (VESIcal “fixedvolatiles”). The original-volatiles starts use the oxides, Fe3+/FeT (0.167) and temperature in data/original_volatiles_2026/starting_conditions.csv. No composition is used for another volcano.
Grid. SR: three compositions (lava AZ09-UK01, scoria AZ09-GCB, inclusion mean) × H2O 2.6, 3.1, 3.55, 4.0, 4.5 wt% × CO2 3141, 5755, 9079 and 14,100 ppm at 1200 °C, plus three runs at 1166 °C and the original-volatiles starts. Cima and Vulcan’s Throne were run on their own compositions only (not used for rates). Pressure steps from the saturation pressure: 10 MPa above 200 MPa, 5 MPa to 20 MPa, 1 MPa to 1 MPa, then 0.5 and 0.1 MPa.
Iacono-Marziano and Dixon (run_fast.py). VESIcal 1.2.12 on the host. Closed system: calculate_degassing_path(fractionate_vapor=0). Open system: one step at a time with CO2 below 1e-6 wt% set to zero, because VESIcal-Dixon can stall in its Redlich–Kwong volume loop once dissolved CO2 reaches about zero (a change of at most 2e-6 wt% H2O). Each path has a 300 s limit, and paths with missing steps are rejected (none occurred).
MagmaSat (queue_magmasat.py, magmasat_path.py, run_magmasat.sh). The ENKI ThermoEngine container (VESIcal 1.2.10), one subprocess per path with a 2 h limit and a per-path cache. Check: run on the exact 2023 pressure list (3.36 wt% H2O, 8528.8 ppm CO2, Fe3+/FeT 0.17, 1200 °C), MagmaSat reproduces the 2023 path file at all 202 rows to 1.1e-4 wt% H2O.
MafiCH (run_mafich.py). The authors’ supplement script, run through a driver copy, with temperature fixed at 1200 °C, 25 ppm CO2 steps and total Fe as FeO. Its paths stop at about 10 ppm CO2 (4–5 MPa closed, 80 MPa open), so they do not reach the final stage.
Dixon normalization. VESIcal’s Dixon model reads SiO2 as given. Scaling the oxides to 100 − H2O − CO2 lowers SiO2 by 1.4–3.0 wt%, which Dixon reads as a more alkaline melt, so the Dixon paths here (hydrous normalization) understate Dixon’s saturation pressures by 11–25 %. Dixon is a sensitivity case only, so this changes no result.
Isotherms and the T-consistent path. In a closed system melt H2O at (P, T) depends only on P, T and the bulk volatiles, so the path along \(T(P) = 1330\ \mathrm{°C} - s\,(2.26\ \mathrm{GPa} - P)\) is the isotherms interpolated linearly in T at T(P) for each P. All 432 fast paths and all 10 new MagmaSat isotherms ran without failures. Control: the 1200 °C-path control reproduces the path fits (olivine 0.089 at 90.4 °C/GPa against 0.090 at 90 °C/GPa).
Xenolith boundary. Unflagged xenolith rows of data/compiled/csv/T1_SIMS_NAMS.csv, medians by xenolith, mineral, position and core or rim. For each path, the pressure at which K × melt H2O falls to the measured value is interpolated; the current-coefficient crossings are from scripts/model_choices/anchoring.py.

title: Appendix D — Data quality
text:
D.1 Calibration
This appendix documents how far the SIMS dataset can be trusted: the calibration lines, what uncertainty is reported and why, the detection limits, the one re-reduced analysis, the electron-microprobe coverage, the disagreements between the deposited text and the data, the checks on the compiled workbook, and the olivine Fo populations. The measurements and their use are in Chapter 4 and Chapter 5.
The calibration question is whether the olivine data and the olivine/melt K that converts them to melt H2O are on the same scale. Scaling the olivine data by a factor s has the same effect on a fitted rate as using K/s, so a mismatch between them would bias the rate directly.
Each analysis is reduced as x = 16O1H/30Si × SiO2 (wt%) of the analysis, with no further division, and H2O (ppm) = slope × x + intercept. Each line is an orthogonal-distance regression of the session’s standards plus its blank rows, with the x error from the ratio scatter and the y error the accepted standard error, followed by a 5000-draw bootstrap.
The per-session standards (glass, olivine, opx and cpx reference materials, plus Suprasil and synthetic forsterite as blanks) are listed in the calibration table of the supplement; the text of the deposited chapter lists 2013-only standards among the 2018 ones [CHECK: per-session standard lists, supplement Table S6 block D]. The NanoSIMS glass line is printed as 143 on the calibration figure against 147.6 recomputed (an old label); the glass line is not used for minerals, so no action was taken.

title: Appendix D — Data quality
text:
The SIMS dataset uses the revised opx standards. Towbin et al. (2023) revised KBH-1 from 217 ± 11 to 202 ± 15 ppm, based on the Bell et al. (1995) manometry (186 ppm measured, plus a 14 % upward correction that the paper treats as a maximum). ROM-273-OG2 (263 to 245) and India enstatite (141 to 131) were revised with it, so earlier opx concentrations scale by 0.93.
Olivine is reduced on the opx line in all sessions. With the revision, the opx SIMS line is 12 % above the Withers (2012) olivine line, against 19 % before. The 2023 paper treats this as within uncertainty.
The olivine/melt K is on the same scale. Towbin et al. (2023) built K by recalibrating the published experiments (Koga 2003, Aubaud 2004, Hauri 2006; Newcombe 2020 inclusion pairs) onto this calibration. The revised mean partition coefficient is 0.0009, the K = 9 ppm per wt% used for the olivine rate.
The remaining calibration uncertainty is the 12 %. Placing the olivine exactly on the Withers (2012) line is equivalent to K ≈ 10.1, which gives about 0.125 MPa/s against 0.155 MPa/s for the isothermal wet-start fit.
Two older scales are superseded, not alternatives. The old Bell calibration (× 1.352 of the SIMS dataset) and the “Withers” column of the 2018 raw workbook (× 0.789) are not used. The workbook column does not match the Withers (2012) line, which would be about 0.89 times the revised opx values; it is probably an older implementation without the blank correction the paper applies. Sensitivity runs on the × 0.789 column (an earlier stall fit) are on a superseded scale.
The pyroxene diffusivities carry their own scale factors (opx × 0.93; a separate cpx factor), treated in Appendix A.

title: Appendix D — Data quality
section: D.2 Total 1σ against the deposited combined uncertainty
text:
D.2 Total 1σ against the deposited combined uncertainty
The deposited “combined uncertainty” is \(\sqrt{((P_{95} - \mathrm{best})^2 + (\mathrm{best} - P_5)^2)/16 + s_{SIMS}^2}\). It reproduces every deposited value but it understates the calibration term: it carries about 0.58 of the calibration 1σ. The SIMS dataset therefore reports the total 1σ
\[
\sigma_{tot} = \sqrt{\sigma_{cal}^2 + \sigma_{count}^2 + \sigma_0^2},
\tag{D.1}\]
where \(\sigma_{cal}\) is the larger side of the 5–95 % calibration interval divided by 1.645, \(\sigma_{count}\) the counting standard error and \(\sigma_0\) the Suprasil blank scatter beyond counting statistics, times the slope. Examples: T1-181 (2.20 ppm) goes from 0.095 to 0.30 ppm, and T1-056 (206 ppm) from 10.5 to 18.8 ppm. The Ol-2 spots carry 0.31–0.43 ppm, and 2013 analyses, which had no uncertainty, now have one. The compiled data also keep the deposited column, renamed “as deposited”. The ascent fits do not read these uncertainties: each fit uses a fixed σ per profile (Section A.3), so the change affects only the reported values. The 2023 edition of the supplement keeps the deposited values.
The calibration term is shared by all points of a session and line, so it acts like a scale (K) error rather than scatter; moving it into the K prior changes nothing visible in the rates (Section A.3).

title: Appendix D — Data quality
text:
D.3 Detection limits
Three limits (Table D.2) are quoted per session and line, computed from the Suprasil blank scatter in the same unit as the samples (x above), with blanks entering at their own SiO2. Suprasil is the near-blank (nominally 1 ± 1 ppm, likely 1–2 ppm); the NanoSIMS synthetic forsterite blank is probably SynFo70, which carries real H, and is not used.



Table D.2: The detection limit is the lowest H2O that is distinguished from the blank 95 % of the time; the quantification limit is the lowest at which the total 1σ is a fifth of the value. Definitions used for the limits of the SIMS H2O data.









Quantity
Definition




Background
Minus the intercept of the session line: the H2O equivalent of the x-intercept. The line removes it; it is a level, not a limit


L_C, decision limit
Hubaux & Vos (1970) with a prediction band: the 95th percentile of bootstrap x-intercepts plus one spot’s Suprasil scatter, read on the best line (one-sided α = 0.05)


L_D, detection limit
The lowest true H2O whose 5th-percentile reading reaches the L_C threshold (α = β = 0.05); equals Currie’s 3.29σ0 for a normal spread


LoQ, quantification limit
The lowest H2O with total 1σ / H2O ≤ 20 %






Each analysis is tagged against L_D and LoQ and every measured value is kept (no substitution). The limits are in Table D.1. Of the 284 analyses, six are below L_D: T1-039 and T1-040 (NanoSIMS cpx, CA18-05) and T1-158 to T1-161 (2013 Cima olivine); T1-135 and T1-136 (NanoSIMS pit cpx) lie between L_D and LoQ; 276 are quantified, including every 2018 olivine. For the 2018 olivine, L_D is 0.99 ppm and LoQ 1.44 ppm. Because the Cima olivine values are below L_D, the SR-to-Cima olivine ratio is not quoted.
The other volatiles are less certain. Blanks from the 6f sessions show that F in pyroxene and P are real signals, while S, Cl and CO2 in these minerals sit at or near the blank level, so their tabulated values are counting statistics only and carry no calibration or blank term. The supplement keeps H2O, F and P as the main volatiles and gives S, Cl and CO2 in one note.

D.4 T1-216 on the opx line
T1-216 (analysis CA18-05x-OPX_Core) is an opx analysis that was reduced at SiO2 55 and, as deposited, not on the opx line. The 2026 edition and the compiled data use its opx-line value, 129.70 ppm (90 % interval 119.93–139.09), from the opx columns of the 2023 processing sheet, against 131.26 ppm as deposited. It is the maximum of the Cima xenolith opx (35–130 ppm in the 2026 edition). The 2023 edition and the figure data keep 131.26.

EMPA supplies the SiO2 used in the SIMS reduction, the Mg# and Cr of the pyroxenes, and the olivine Fo profiles. Coverage is uneven.

SR. The compiled EMPA table has one analysis per SR xenolith: cpx Mg# 91.7 (GCB1), 90.9 (WHT1) and 92.5 (WHT06_1). Per-grain 2018 data for GCB1 were recovered (82 points; 9 cpx and 7 opx grains linked to SIMS grains) and added as a separate table. The GCB1 grains are uniform: cpx Mg# 91.3–91.8, opx 90.3–90.4.
