No usable EMPA exists for VT8504, VT8505, VT8506, VT8536, VT8535 cluster 3, cip98-19 clusters 1, 8 and 10, CA18-05x, CA18-Lavablock, or the WHT06_2 xenolith grains, after a search of every EMPA session found.

Ol-2 grew early, from a more primitive melt. Its core plateau sits about 3 Fo units above lava equilibrium and above every WHT06 phenocryst core except ol40 (88.1–88.2). It was then re-equilibrated toward the carrier from the rim. A late, shallow origin is unlikely, which supports starting the H2O model in equilibrium with the deep melt.

title: Appendix D — Data quality
text:
D.9 Measurement methods
SIMS and NanoSIMS. The SR xenolith sections, scoria phenocrysts and xenocrysts were analyzed on the Cameca 6f SIMS at the Carnegie Institution for Science in 2018 (GCB1 and its scoria) and on the Cameca NanoSIMS at Caltech in 2020 (WHT01 and WHT06, Mounts A and B). The Cima and Vulcan’s Throne samples were analyzed on the Carnegie 6f in 2013, following Lloyd et al. (2013) and Newcombe et al. (2020). The 2013 session could not measure olivine above background routinely, and the 2020 session had too high a background for olivine, so 48 of the 52 olivine analyses are from 2018. Samples were cleaned in acetone, toluene, distilled water and isopropanol baths, with only acetone-soluble plastics used in preparation, mounted in indium, held at 90 °C under vacuum for 2 days and held under ultrahigh vacuum (10^-9 Torr) for 72 hours before analysis. A Cs+ beam measured 16O1H, 12C, 19F, 31P, 32S and 35Cl relative to 30Si. Calibration curves were built for each phase from standards analyzed in the same session. Other protocols followed Towbin et al. (2023), including the revised opx standard values.
EMPA. Major elements were measured on the Cameca SX100 at the American Museum of Natural History in 2018 (GCB1) and on the Cameca Tactis in several sessions from summer 2020 to February 2022 (protocols as in Chapter 2). The GCB1 per-grain data were recovered from the July 2018 workbook and checked point by point against the raw instrument export. Phases were assigned by composition (cpx CaO ≥ 15 wt%; opx CaO < 3 and MgO 28–37 wt%); Mg# is molar with all Fe as FeO.
Olivine Fo populations. The script reads the “Olivine” sheet of the melt-vein EMPA master workbook with bad and ignored points removed, assigns each profile to a population (phenocryst, xenocryst in scoria, WHT1 exterior grain, melt-pocket overgrowth, xenolith olivine), takes the core Fo as the median beyond 70 % of the profile length and the rim Fo as the analysis nearest the edge. Olivine in equilibrium with the AZ09-UK01 lava was computed for Fe3+/FeT 0.167–0.20 and Kd 0.30–0.34 (Fo 83.6–85.7).

text:
E.1 Decisions
This appendix is the record behind the report: the decisions taken and their evidence, the 41 claims of the deposited Chapter 3 against their 2026 status, the scripts that regenerate every number, and the dated working logs the chapters were written from. Dates and working-document names appear only here.
Table E.1 lists the choices behind the central rate and the report, sorted by date. Letter-number codes (A1, B4, D5) are the question numbers of the supplement question list; “plan answer” refers to the answers recorded for the summary workbook; “review section 9” is the set of decisions on the rebuilt report.
The newest decisions change the framing more than the numbers. The headline is now the joint fit of olivine, opx and cpx on the P–T path (0.100 MPa/s, 0.050–0.200 over 46–120 °C/GPa, MiMiC start) rather than the olivine-only 0.093 MPa/s; continuous ascent is the best history at the central and steepest slopes (a 5-minute stall fits better only at 46 °C/GPa); the published MiMiC melt replaced the CO2/Nb start as the primary start on 2026-10-30; and the report leads with what changed since the 2023 chapter.

section: E.2 Crosswalk to the deposited Chapter 3
text:
E.2 Crosswalk to the deposited Chapter 3
The deposited Chapter 3 (Testing the Fidelity of Peridotite Xenoliths as Records of Water in the Lithospheric Mantle) is the 2023 baseline. Table E.2 lists its substantive claims, results and interpretations in the order of the chapter and gives each a status against the 2026 analyses:

Confirmed: the 2026 work supports the point.
Revised: the point stands in outline but the number or the method changed.
Superseded: the 2026 work replaces it.
Extended: the point stands and was tested further.
Not revisited: the 2026 sources do not address it.

Statuses rest on the working logs in Section E.4. The text-versus-data conflicts that predate this work (the olivine sentences read about 1.3 times the SIMS dataset values) are in Section D.6. No value of the SIMS dataset was changed.



Table E.2: Chapter 3 claims against the 2026 analyses. Of 41 points, 20 are revised, 7 confirmed, 7 extended, 2 superseded and 5 not revisited; the largest changes are the degassing onset, the starting melt and the ascent rate.











#
Chapter 3 point (section)
Status in 2026
What changed, and where




1
Question: do xenolith NAMs diffusively equilibrate with the host magma, tested against the host magma’s own P, T, H2O and degassing path (Abstract; Introduction)
Confirmed
Same question; 2026 frames it as H+ exchange between xenolith and host, then degassing and water loss (Chapter 1).


2
Four-stage framework: Stage 0 mantle, Stage I ascent in undersaturated magma, Stage II ascent in degassing magma, Stage III post-eruption (Introduction)
Revised
Stages restated as mantle start (1330 °C, 2.26 GPa), xenolith pickup (about 1.15 GPa), saturation and degassing, diffusive loss that records the rate, and quench (Chapter 1, Chapter 3).


3
Xenolith entrained at about 1.2 GPa (40 km), from Chapter 2 (Discussion, Stage I)
Confirmed
Pickup at about 1.15 GPa under hotter conditions, where the melt is H2O-undersaturated (Chapter 9).


4
Sullivan Ranch xenoliths GCB1, WHT01 and WHT06 with host scoria treated as one sample set (Methods, Sample Descriptions)
Extended
Two localities, probably two magma pulses: pit (WHT06, AZ18-06 inclusions) and roadside (GCB1, WHT01, GC2 inclusions); path kept SR-wide (Appendix D).


5
SIMS calibration and protocols follow Towbin et al. (2023) (Methods, SIMS)
Revised
The SIMS dataset has the olivine on the revised opx calibration (KBH-1 = 202 ppm), within about 12 % of the Withers (2012) line; the older Bell and workbook-Withers scales are superseded (Appendix D).


6
Interior olivine cores 6–12 ppm (avg 9), exterior cores 6–8 (avg 7), phenocryst cores 8–11 (avg 9) (Results, Olivine)
Revised
The SIMS dataset gives 6.89, 5.95 and 6.77 ppm (about 1.3× lower); the text predates the Feb 2023 recalibration. Interior, exterior and phenocryst cores still overlap (Appendix D).


7
Olivine cores across the xenolith equal the phenocryst cores, evidence of equilibration with the host (Results, Olivine; Abstract)
Confirmed
Pattern broadly holds in the SIMS dataset (interior 6.89, exterior 5.95, phenocryst 6.77 ppm); the 2026 working hypothesis is that the host reset the NAMs (Chapter 1, Appendix D).


8
Olivine rims lower than cores by about 1.5 ppm; lowest rims 3–4 ppm; rim concentrations of phenocrysts and xenolith overlap at 5–7 ppm (Results, Olivine)
Revised
The SIMS dataset: lowest rims 2.2–3.6 ppm; mean rims 4.6 (xenolith) and 3.6 (phenocryst); not a simple scale factor (Appendix D).


9
Phenocryst and xenolith olivine profiles nearly identical, about 10 to 6 ppm over under 100 µm (Fig. 3c)
Revised
The SIMS dataset gives the phenocryst profile as 7.9 to 4.4 ppm; the rate is set by the scoria phenocryst Ol-2 profiled along [100]. The profile length scale supports the same ascent signal in both (Chapter 8).


10
FTIR olivine speciation: site-specific OH peaks differ between interior, exterior and phenocryst olivine (Results, Fig. 4)
Not revisited
FTIR is out of scope; a likely diffusion–reaction side story within the xenolith is left as future work.


11
Cpx 65–500 ppm; no relation between Mg# and H2O (Results, Clinopyroxene)
Revised
The SIMS dataset range is 62.6–594 ppm including Vulcan’s Throne (63–488 without); cpx values rest on the recalibrated scale (Appendix D).


12
Cpx zoned in NanoSIMS (30 % drop in outer 70 µm); every SIMS spot within 50 µm of the rim is lower than the core (Results, Clinopyroxene)
Not revisited
Interpretation kept; the text-versus-data check lists two exceptions (GCB1 R-31 CPX-4, CA18-05x) (Appendix D).


13
Opx more strongly zoned than cpx; most rims over 100 ppm below cores; wider zone of loss (Results, Orthopyroxene)
Revised
The SIMS dataset: 3 of 10 opx grains with core and rim differ by over 100 ppm (cpx 2 of 11) (Appendix D).


14
WHT1 opx rims fall toward the exterior (about 100 ppm) and approach cores in the interior (about 300 ppm) (Results; Discussion, Stage II)
Revised
Exterior opx rim 158 ppm (median of the exterior rims; 96 ppm is the outermost spot of the modeled grain), interior 209–242 ppm in the SIMS dataset; intact interior opx cores (about 411 ppm) now anchor the start, and the exterior opx is effectively unbuffered (Chapter 8).


15
Sullivan Ranch magma has at least 3.4 wt% H2O (maximum inclusion), Vulcan’s Throne 2.3, Cima 1.5, taken as the Stage I magma (Results, Melt Inclusions)
Revised
Primary start is the published MiMiC melt (Ol23, 3.549 wt% H2O, 8,529 ppm CO2); the wettest-melt CO2/Nb start SR-1 (3.59 wt% H2O, 14,100 ppm CO2) is the second scenario; Cima and Vulcan’s Throne are separate volcanoes with their own melts and are not used for the rate (Chapter 6).


16
MIMiC restores bubble CO2: about 8,500 ppm CO2 and 500 MPa for Sullivan Ranch (Results, Melt Inclusions)
Revised
Original MIMiC reproduced exactly (max difference 0.005); modified production run with Duan and Zhang (2006) bubble CO2 raises SR CO2 by 0–15 % and Pvbg by 0–8 %; SR Pvbg 212–574 MPa (Chapter 6).


17
Degassing path from MagmaSat: no water leaves the magma until below 150 MPa (6 km) (Results, Fig. 8b)
Superseded
The MiMiC start saturates at 682 MPa on the MagmaSat path; the melt retains 90 % at 248 MPa, loses half below about 55 MPa and retains 25 % at 16 MPa (CO2/Nb start: 922 MPa, 341 MPa, 63 MPa, 17 MPa) (Appendix C).


18
Starting melt of the degassing path: GCB lava (3.36 wt% H2O, 8,476 ppm CO2, 1200 °C; implied from the 2023 path)
Superseded
The 2023 path is reproduced exactly (AZ09-UK01 with Fe3+/FeT 0.170) but replaced by the published MiMiC start (second scenario: the CO2/Nb start SR-1); the drier 2.72 wt% mixture is kept as a sensitivity case (Appendix C, Chapter 6).


19
H2O correlates with Cl, S and SiO2 in SR inclusions, so the variation is primary melt heterogeneity, not degassing or diffusion (Results, Fig. 9)
Confirmed
2026 data are consistent with primary melt batches; among Fo 84–86 hosts H2O follows Cl; the H2O–Fo trend is weak (r = 0.54, carried by Ol36) (Chapter 6).


20
Average SR host-magma H2O of 2.6 ± 0.5 wt% from the H2O–SiO2 correlation (Results, Fig. 9b)
Revised
Mixture batch of 2.72 wt% describes the inclusion population, but the MiMiC melt (3.549 wt%) is the primary start because the interior opx cores imply 3.48 wt% (Chapter 6, Chapter 8).


21
SR inclusions all trapped in Fo 85–87 olivine (Results, Melt Inclusions)
Revised
Hosts are Fo 84.2–86.1 (pit) and 84.7–86.2 (roadside), plus Ol36 at Fo 79.3–79.7; 5 of 13 inclusions are below Fo 85 (Chapter 6).


22
Post-eruptive cooling (Stage III) has little effect on bulk NAM water; bombs close in under 5 to 15 minutes (Discussion, Stage III; Abstract)
Extended
Post-eruptive holds were tested as a scenario: survival of the Ol-2 profile limits any hold to well under about 3.6 min (Section A.9).


23
Decompression rate from the Ol-2 phenocryst, Newcombe method: 0.2 ± 0.05 MPa/s (central core) or 0.16 ± 0.02 (equilibrium core) (Discussion, Stage II)
Revised
Olivine-only 0.093 (0.055–0.154) MPa/s on the P–T path (about 3.4 m/s) and 0.143 (0.108–0.193) isothermal at 1200 °C; the headline is the joint fit of olivine, opx and cpx on the path, 0.100 MPa/s (0.050–0.200 over 46–120 °C/GPa; about 3.6 m/s) (Chapter 8).


24
Olivine/melt partition coefficient 0.0009 from Towbin et al. (2023); Fig. 11 caption prints 0.009 ± 0.003 (Discussion, Stage I; Fig. 11)
Confirmed
K = 9 ppm per wt% is kept as the primary; the caption value is a typo for 0.0009 ± 0.0003. Peterson’s speciation-based D is a sensitivity (0.146 MPa/s, 0.94×) (Appendix A).


25
Isothermal at about 1200 °C throughout (Discussion; Implications)
Revised
Temperature falls along a straight P–T path from 1330 °C at 2.26 GPa (slope U(46, 120) °C/GPa) to about 1176 °C at the surface; this lowers every rate by 0.63–0.69× and equals an isothermal fit at about 1150 °C (Chapter 9, Chapter 8).


26
A single crystal gives the most robust Stage II rate, with a caveat about crystal populations (Barth et al., 2019) (Discussion, Stage II)
Extended
Ol-2 is a scoria phenocryst; plausible range 0.03–0.4 MPa/s; stalls, edge effects, other D laws and the Fo populations are tested (Appendix A).


27
Rate is similar to Seguam 1977 and Cerro Negro 1992 (Barth 2019) (Discussion, Stage II)
Revised
Now 1.0× Seguam 1977 (was 1.5×) and 3.4–11× faster than the Cerro Negro olivine rates; 0.21× the Etna 3930 BP analog (Chapter 8).


28
Olivine zonation length scale identical in xenolith and phenocryst implies fast grain-boundary and melt-vein transport (Discussion, Stage II)
Extended
The data need a fast, low-storage pathway (fluid-wetted boundaries or cracks) carrying the signal inward with a lag (Chapter 8).


29
Pyroxene profiles agree with about 0.2 MPa/s at the low end of experimental diffusivities (Discussion, Stage II; Fig. 11e,f, Fig. 12)
Confirmed
Joint fit with the MiMiC start (chi-square 20.0 isothermal, 20.6 on the path, 20 points) needs opx D near 10^-11.0 and cpx near 10^-11.5 m²/s at 1200 °C (−10.98 and −11.50 on the path), slow natural-pyroxene values; the single-mineral pyroxene rates on the path are 0.161 (opx) and 0.50 (cpx) MPa/s (Appendix A, Chapter 8).


30
Effective grain-boundary transport across WHT1: log D of -6 to -5.5 m²/s; grain-boundary log D -4.8 to -4.3 via Demouchy et al. (2010) (Discussion, Fig. 13)
Revised
On the MiMiC P–T path at the joint rate the nested network D is 10^-5.6 m²/s (−5.8 to −5.6) and the coupled fit gives −5.50; across every joint-fit scenario the network D is 10^-5.4 to −6.0, 1.6–5 times below the Demouchy et al. (2010) olivine grain-boundary value (5 × 10^-6 m²/s) (Chapter 8).


31
For molten Sullivan Ranch xenoliths the rate is dominated by the fast grain-boundary path (Discussion, Stage II)
Extended
Melt network (D_melt about 5e-10), grain boundaries and hybrids compared; Demouchy regimes A/B/C placed with grain boundaries dominant on the loss path (Chapter 8).


32
Stage I lasts at least about 100 minutes at 0.2 MPa/s, or about 6 days at the Chapter 2 week-long minimum (0.002 MPa/s) (Discussion, Stage I)
Extended
Fe–Mg times with FORSTER: Ol-2 18 d (16–21) in the final carrier melt; xenocrysts 0.15–3.0 d, reproducing the thesis times within a factor of 2 (new fits shorter). The one-week entrainment total is not recomputed (Chapter 9).


33
Cpx (500 µm) fully equilibrates with the host in about 7 hours at 1200 °C, so all minerals reset in a week (Discussion, Stage I)
Not revisited
Not recomputed in the 2026 sources; the wet-start test supports reset for opx (Chapter 8).


34
Cpx cores consistent with equilibrium partitioning, D about 0.005–0.02, matching O’Leary eq. 10 given IVAl (Discussion, Fig. 15)
Revised
Cpx D refit to experiments on the common SIMS scale. The observed ÷ predicted cpx D is 1.29–1.84 for the three SR xenoliths (2.61 Vulcan’s Throne, 1.19 Cima), so the cores hold 1.2–2.6 times the water the experiments predict; WHT1 and Cima are within 1σ of the maximum melt H2O, WHT06_1 1.7σ, GCB1 2.5σ and Vulcan’s Throne 2.7σ. The Cr-Tschermak adjustment changes D by only 3–7 %. Left open (Chapter 9, Chapter 11).


35
Olivine cores of about 9 ppm are in equilibrium with 1 wt% melt H2O (D = 0.0009) (Discussion, Stage I)
Revised
The SIMS dataset interior mean is 6.9 ppm (implied D about 0.0007); D falls with melt H2O in the speciation-based alternative (1.04e-3 at 0.4 wt%, 0.55e-3 at 3.55 wt%) (Appendix A).


36
Ascent overprints the mantle water: no vestige of Stage 0 is retained (Discussion, Stage 0; Abstract)
Confirmed
Under the reset hypothesis the intact interior opx cores imply 3.48 wt% melt H2O, within 2 % of the MiMiC start and 3 % of SR-1; the cpx partitioning check is open (Chapter 8, Chapter 8).


37
Hot alkali basalts of cinder cones are the worst case for xenolith water fidelity; cooler, faster magmas (kimberlites) may preserve it (Implications)
Not revisited
No new constraint on other magma types in the 2026 sources.


38
Xenoliths are time keepers: ascent accelerates from 0.002 MPa/s (a week from the Moho) to 0.2 MPa/s in the upper crust (Implications, Fig. 16)
Revised
Upper-crust rate is now about 0.10 MPa/s on the P–T path; the 0.002 MPa/s deep rate comes from Chapter 2 and is not recomputed (Chapter 8, Chapter 9).


39
Published xenolith-NAM ascent velocities (Demouchy et al., 2006) pertain to Stage II, not the whole ascent (Implications)
Extended
Published xenolith-NAM rates assume loss from entrainment with a fixed zero boundary, not a degassing boundary, so they are upper bounds and not like-for-like (Chapter 8).


40
Three volcanoes compared on the same footing: Sullivan Ranch, Vulcan’s Throne, Cima (Abstract; Methods)
Revised
SR, Cima and Vulcan’s Throne are separate volcanoes that never share a starting melt, FeO or Fe3+/FeT; the ascent-rate work is SR only (Appendix D, Chapter 6).


41
Colorado Plateau and Basin and Range xenolith water contents (Li et al., 2008) need re-evaluation because Grand Canyon magmas are wet (about 3 wt%) (Implications)
Not revisited
SR melt of 3.59 wt% is consistent with a wet magma, but the broader argument is not re-examined.






New in 2026 (not in Chapter 3).

Temperature along the magma P–T path. A straight path from 1330 ± 15 °C at 2.26 ± 0.10 GPa; the families (Towbin and Plank 2026, a fit through 12 SR inclusions, and the SR-wide envelope) give 1176 to 1107 °C at the surface and slow every rate by a common factor (Chapter 3, Chapter 8).
Localities and magma pulses. Pit and roadside samples are probably different pulses; roadside inclusions are hotter at the same pressure (1148–1198 against 1139–1166 °C).
Fe–Mg residence times and Fo populations. FORSTER times for Ol-2 (18 d) and the xenocrysts, rims in equilibrium with the lava, and the lower-MgO final melt that no measured inclusion samples (Section A.10, Section D.8).
MiMiC versions. Original (reproduced exactly), 2026 baseline and modified (Duan & Zhang bubble CO2) runs; the version moves the ascent rates by 2 % or less and the P–T slope by 0.2 °C/GPa (Appendix B).
Solubility temperature. Evaluating MagmaSat along isotherms of 1050–1300 °C changes the rate by 3 % or less (Section C.4).
Literature model temperatures. Each published rate placed on its own model temperature, so the SR rate is compared like for like (Chapter 8).
Interior-core anchoring of the start. Intact interior WHT1 opx cores fix the starting melt H2O at 3.48 wt%, within 2 % of the MiMiC start (3.549) and 3 % of SR-1; two grains flatten near 300–320 ppm, which is treated as a K or starting-H2O uncertainty (Chapter 9).
Joint fit with free pyroxene D, on the P–T path. One continuous ascent fits olivine, opx and cpx at 0.100 MPa/s; no stall is needed at the central slope (Chapter 8, Section A.9).
Uncertainty and detection limits. Total 1σ, L_C, L_D and LoQ for every analysis; fixed fit σ kept (Appendix D).
Barth edge effects on olivine. Two-population models fit Ol-2 only if exchange is fast, and widening the final-pressure prior moves the isothermal rate only within 0.155–0.164 MPa/s on the CO2/Nb start (Section A.8).
Alternative olivine laws and solubility models. Peterson D_OH and power law, Barth laws, and Iacono-Marziano against MagmaSat (Appendix A, Appendix C).
Grain-boundary fits and mechanisms. Coupled and nested grain-boundary fits on the joint-fit scenarios, buffering of the exterior grains, and the melt, grain-boundary and hybrid pathways (Chapter 8).
Cpx partitioning misfit and CO2/Nb. The cpx cores hold 1.2–2.6 times the water the recalibrated experiments predict; the start CO2 is a CO2/Nb estimate (Chapter 9, Section B.7).

title: Appendix E — Decisions, crosswalk and reproducibility
text:
E.3 Reproducibility: scripts, outputs, commands
One table per topic lists the script, what it does and where its output goes. All paths are relative to the repository root (Ch3_Xenolith_SIMS_Clean, private). Each script’s module docstring gives its command; the patterns are below. Scripts without a documented purpose, shared helpers and FTIR scripts (scripts/ftir/, out of scope) are not listed. The dated working documents that describe these runs are in Section E.4.
The external code the scripts call is in Table E.3.
Environments.

NAM environment (all decompression fits). The posterior code lives in the H2O_Diffusion_NAM repository (public). Fit scripts in scripts/decompression/ run as PYTHONPATH=~/Projects/H2O_Diffusion_NAM uv run --project ~/Projects/H2O_Diffusion_NAM --with pyarrow --with scipy python scripts/decompression/<script>.py. Plot-only scripts need only uv run --with pandas --with matplotlib.
MagmaSat degassing paths (container). MagmaSat runs inside the ENKI ThermoEngine container (VESIcal 1.2.10). scripts/degassing_paths/run_magmasat.sh [N] starts N parallel containers (through colima and docker), skips cached paths, and writes JSON files to data/degassing_paths_2026/magmasat/cache/. The fast models (Iacono-Marziano, Dixon) run on the host with --with VESIcal==1.2.12.
MiMiC. The vendored code in scripts/mimic/vendor/ (Rasmussen et al. 2020) is unmodified (PROVENANCE.md records the upstream commit). scripts/mimic/run_mimic.py runs it with uv run --no-project --python 3.13 --with numpy==2.2.6 --with scipy==1.16.3.
Fe–Mg diffusion. FORSTER, from the Olivine_Diffusion_FeMg repository: uv run --project ~/Projects/Olivine_Diffusion_FeMg forster fit ....
Everything else uses uv run --with <packages> or the project .venv as in each script’s docstring.

text:
F.8 Figure 12: decompression rate against diffusivity










Figure 12 (Chapter 3). Left (a): as deposited (2023). Right (b): replica with the 2026 single-mineral fits (published MiMiC start, P-T path): log diffusivity against log decompression rate for olivine, opx and cpx. Each cloud is 150 draws, as in the deposited figure: the diffusivity uniform within the mineral’s diffusivity bracket (the laws at T − 20 K and T + 20 K) and the rate scaled from that mineral’s fit with its 68 % spread; shaded bands are the 68 % envelopes. The joint-fit rate (0.100 MPa/s) and the pyroxene diffusivities it implies (opx −11.00, cpx −11.50) are marked.

Figure 12, 2026 form. The pyroxene diffusivities one ascent history needs, against published laws. Every published law on it was checked against its source (docs/literature/VERIFY_FIG12_FIG16_2026-10-30.md): all 24 recompute to the plotted 1200 °C value within 0.002 log units. 21 were read in full text. The three Hercule & Ingrin (1999) laws were checked against the abstract only (the paper is not in the Zotero library), and the log D0 of −3.4 for their [001]/[100] law is not confirmed. The D0 exponents of Carpenter (2003) are illegible in the thesis scan; the laws match that thesis’s plotted data to about 0.3 log units. Every law is extrapolated 100–350 °C beyond its experiments to reach 1200 °C.
The olivine cloud is tight because its diffusivity bracket is narrow (0.13 log units, against 0.74 for opx and 1.17 for cpx), in 2023 as now. In 2023 each mineral gave its own rate for an assumed diffusivity. In 2026 the joint fit asks which diffusivities let one ascent history fit olivine, opx and cpx together (Chapter 8).

title: Appendix F — Chapter 3 figures, deposited and recompiled
section: F.9 Figure 13: grain-boundary transport across WHT1
text:
F.9 Figure 13: grain-boundary transport across WHT1










Figure 13 (Chapter 3). Left (a): as deposited (2023). Right (b): replica with the 2026 network fitted to each opx grain’s extrapolated rim (published MiMiC start, P–T path 82.8 °C/GPa, 0.100 MPa/s; edge follows the melt): (a) the extrapolated rims (squares, ±1σ), the measured outermost points (circles, 19–45 µm inside the grains) and the network at the end of ascent for the best fit and its 68 % range, scaled to the median opx core (312 ppm); diamonds are each grain’s prediction, its own core times the network’s remaining fraction; (b) the network diffusivity against rate for the two standard fits: the extrapolated rims (log D 10^−6.25, 68 %: −6.35 to −6.15, χ² 5.6 for 4 rims) and option B (all 35 points, one common start, an opx diffusivity per grain: −5.75, −5.81 to −5.68, χ² 44), with the fit to the measured outermost points (−6.45, χ² 26) for comparison, Demouchy et al. (2010) grain-boundary values on a right axis giving the equivalent grain-boundary D from their eq. 5 as the thesis used it (boundary width 10 µm, grain size 500 µm: +1.22 log units), and the Thomaidis (2022) minimum; (c) each grain’s profile with its one-step fit and extrapolated rim.

Figure 13, 2026 form. Transport mechanisms into the xenolith.
The 2023 test treated the measured outermost points as grain-boundary values; it cannot fit both the 0.5 mm and the 40.8 mm grains (χ² 26 for 4 grains). The replica instead extrapolates each grain’s own profile to its edge (scripts/decompression/gb_rim_extrapolated.py: a one-step profile Cb + (C0 − Cb) erf(x/L) with the core C0 held at the grain’s median, ±20 ppm per point), then fits the network to those edges: log D 10^−6.25 (−6.35 to −6.15), χ² 5.6 for 4 rims. Each grain’s prediction is its core (0.5 mm grain 315 ppm, 7.5 mm 264, 40.5 mm 413, 40.8 mm 310) times the network’s remaining fraction. The second standard fit, option B (scripts/decompression/gb_aniso_halfwidth.py), models diffusion inside every grain behind the network with one common start (388 ppm, 384–400) and one opx partition coefficient, and gives each grain its own opx diffusivity for anisotropy: 10^−5.75 (−5.81 to −5.68), χ² 43.8 for 35 points (Chapter 8). Per-grain opx log D: 0.5 mm −11.1, 7.5 mm −11.0, 40.5 mm −11.8, 40.8 mm −10.4. The earlier nested fit, each grain starting at its own measured core with one shared opx D, gave 10^−5.6 (χ² 63.3). A one-step profile treats the falling edge as constant, which biases the extrapolated value low, so the two standard fits bracket the network diffusivity.
The cpx and a fit with every grain (scripts/decompression/gb_all_grains.py, Table F.1). The same extrapolation works poorly for the WHT1 cpx. The 1.45 mm and 40.2 mm grains show a drop at their outermost point only, so their edges are unconstrained. The 7.5 mm and 38.1 mm traverses scatter (one-step χ² 30 for 14 points and 68 for 11), and the 38.1 mm grain’s points labeled Core (298 ppm) sit below its deeper points (about 400). Where it can be read, the cpx rim drops less than the opx rim at the same depth: at 7.5 mm by 27 % against 50 %. Fitted alone, the cpx rims want a network more than ten times slower (−7.35). A full nested fit with all eight grains puts the cpx diffusivity at 10^−13.1, below every published cpx law at 1200 °C (the slowest is −12.77, Ferriss et al. 2016) and 1.6 log units below the joint fit’s −11.5; two scattered cpx traverses supply 148 of its χ² of 227. The cpx therefore do not add a usable constraint on the network, and Figure 13 uses the opx only.

The cpx under option B, alone and with the opx (scripts/decompression/gb_cpx_option_b.py, Table F.2, Figure F.1). Each phase gets one common start (its own absolute partition coefficient) and each grain its own diffusivity; the cpx boundary sees a fraction β of the network’s drop. With β = 1 the cpx fit poorly (χ² 178 for 41 points in the joint fit). With β free the joint opx + cpx fit picks β = 0.5 and a network of 10^−5.6 (χ² 141 for 76 points: cpx 93, opx 48, the opx 3.7 above their own best). Its common starts, 412 ppm for opx and 388 ppm for cpx, match the intact interior cores (411 and 390 ppm) without being told to. The exterior cpx (1.45 and 7.5 mm) and the exterior opx all need log D ≈ −11.0. The interior grains split as the opx do: the 40.2 mm cpx needs −12.6 and the 38.1 mm cpx −11.3. Fitted alone, the cpx cannot separate β from the network diffusivity (β 0.5 with the network at the top of the grid). Most of the remaining cpx misfit is in the scattered 7.5 and 38.1 mm traverses (χ² 33 and 40).

Not yet tested (Henry, 2026-10-31): a path-length factor on each grain’s distance to the exterior, which could make the 40.5 mm grain effectively deeper (it lost less than its depth predicts) but cannot explain the 40.8 mm grain (it lost more; docs/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md Q33).
The 0.5 mm grain’s outermost point is modeled too high (152 against 96 ppm at 21 µm), and the edge value is not the cause. At the end of ascent the network edge has already fallen to about 5 ppm opx-equivalent (98 % of the melt’s drop). Holding the edge at a floor of 50–100 ppm is allowed by the data (χ² 63.6–66.0 against 63.3; 68 % range of the floor 0–75 ppm) but raises the modeled point to 153–168 ppm. Giving that grain its own opx D does not fix it either (best 10^-11.5, modeled point 142 ppm). Its measured profile (96, 207, 273, 308, 321 ppm from 21 to 140 µm) drops more steeply at the rim than one diffusivity from a 315 ppm start allows. The joint fit’s opx D (10^-11.0) is not comparable, because it starts the grain at the 411 ppm interior cores. Holding the edge at a final pressure or a buffering fraction also converges to the unbuffered edge (best Pf = 0, 68 % 0–10 MPa; best f = 1.0, 0.97–1.0).
Why the 2026 fit does not reproduce the deposited panel a. The thesis model (data/recovered/M14_ModelCode/.../WHT1 All opx Grain Bound/master_script_test.m) differs in three choices. Table F.3 reruns it with one choice changed at a time (scripts/decompression/thesis_gb_repro.py).

It treats the five rims (96, 158, 170, 209, 242 ppm) as the grain-boundary concentration itself, with no diffusion inside the grains. The 2026 nested fit puts each measured point 21–45 µm inside a grain that diffuses slowly.
Its edge follows the melt only down to a final pressure Pf drawn from 0–20 MPa, and the run stops there, so the edge ends at K × H(Pf): up to about 90 ppm at 20 MPa. The 2026 edge follows the melt to the surface (about 5 ppm).
It leaves out the 40.5 mm grain’s rim (343 ppm), which sits 100–130 ppm above the other two interior rims at the same depth; no one-dimensional slab can fit both.

The degassing path (VesiCal at 1200 °C in the thesis, MiMiC start now) changes nothing.



Table F.3: The thesis panel is reproduced (rims 95, 145, 241 against 96, 158/170, 209/242) once the rims are treated as grain-boundary values and the edge stops near 20 MPa; the edge stopping at the surface or the 343 ppm rim is what breaks it. So the 96 ppm exterior rim fits only if the xenolith edge stopped exchanging with the melt at about 20–30 MPa, which leaves the edge at 90–115 ppm; the deposited curves end at 60–100 ppm. The nested fit reads the same rim differently: the edge goes to near zero and the grain lags behind it. That reading cannot reach 96 ppm at 21 µm, and it rejects an edge stopping above about 10 MPa.
The 0.5 mm grain: two readings. Every 2026 fit models this grain’s outermost point (96 ppm at 21 µm) too high, the only modeled point well above the data. Two ways to fix it fit about equally well (Table F.4) and leave the network and opx diffusivities unchanged; Figure F.2 compares them.

A, the rim as the boundary value (scripts/decompression/gb_rim_anchor.py). The 96 ppm point is compared with the network concentration at 0.5 mm at the end of ascent; the grain’s inner points are still modeled behind that boundary. The data then prefer an edge that stops falling at about 100 ppm (68 %: 100–125 ppm), or that sees about 70 % of the melt’s drop: a buffered grain boundary.
B, time at a zero edge (scripts/decompression/exterior_grain_tests.py). The grain’s six points form a one-step diffusion profile whose edge is −4 ± 43 ppm (χ² 0.2; ±20 ppm per point); holding that edge at 96 ppm worsens the fit (χ² 7.6) and puts the 21 µm point at 147 ppm. On the melt-controlled history the edge is below 50 ppm for only about 35 s before ascent ends; adding 240 s at a zero edge after ascent (1200 °C reference) fits the grain at the shared opx D. The hold reaches less than 1 mm into the network, so the other grains are unchanged.

(a) The grain’s six SIMS points (±20 ppm, as used in the fits) against the current nested fit, reading A (rim compared with the boundary value, edge buffered at 100 ppm; its modeled profile is the line, its outermost point is scored at the edge), reading B (240 s at a zero edge after ascent), and one-step profiles with the edge free or held at 96 ppm. (b) The edge of that grain over the last 60 MPa of ascent for each reading. MiMiC start, P–T path 82.8 °C/GPa, 0.100 MPa/s, log D_gb −5.6, log D_opx −11.6.



Neither cause is tested yet. Reading A needs a buffer that holds the boundary near 100 ppm: exchange with melt in the veins, or a lag in the network. Reading B needs the grain’s edge to sit near zero for a few minutes at magmatic temperature. That could be hot residence after fragmentation before the bomb quenched (applied consistently, this would also act on the Ol-2 olivine). It could also be a traverse orientation about 0.6 log units faster than the other grains (within published opx anisotropy, e.g. Carpenter 2003 [001] against [100]), or an oblique section that stretches the profile.
The Thomaidis (2022) minimum is the Arrhenius fit through the strongest lower limit at 600, 700 and 900 °C in his Table 6.5 (Ea 140 kJ/mol), extrapolated to 1200 °C: log D = −7.76, as the thesis text quotes (−7.8); the deposited figure drew it at −6.6. Thomaidis derived these limits from d = √(D_gb t), the time for the boundaries to deliver deuterium to an opx at distance d, and notes that they need no assumption about the boundary width (his p. 73). They are therefore the same kind of quantity as the fitted network D and are drawn as published on the network axis; the eq. 5 rescaling would move both by the same 1.22 log units, so the fit stays 2.2 log units above the minimum. On the grain-boundary axis the fit is −4.4 (68 %: −4.6 to −4.4), at Demouchy’s printed law (−4.61) and 0.9 log units above its tabulated value (−5.29), as the thesis text found (−4.8 to −4.3).

F.10 Figure 14: time for a cpx to equilibrate with the host










Figure 14 (Chapter 3). Left (a): as deposited (2023). Right (b): replica with the 2026 cpx diffusivity (joint fit, log10 D = −11.50 m²/s at 1200 °C), same 500 µm slab and analytic solution.
At the deposited diffusivity (log10 D = −11.3) the same calculation reproduces the deposited times (13 min and 6.8 h against 14 min and 7 h). With the slower 2026 cpx diffusivity the center reaches 1 % of the change in 21 min, 90 % in 5.7 h and 99 % in 10.8 h, about 1.6 times the deposited 7 h. Full equilibration still takes far less than the days of residence in the carrier (Chapter 9).

text:
F.11 Figure 15: cpx cores against the host-magma water










Figure 15 (Chapter 3). Left (a): as deposited (2023). Right (b): replica with the 2026 values: (a) cpx cores against the best melt H2O of each volcano (bars: best-estimate range) with lines of constant D; for Vulcan’s Throne and Cima the bar runs up to the soft maximum from literature H2O/Ce (upper value 265; Rasmussen 2017, Rowe 2015, Dixon 2017) times Ce: 3.23 wt% (Vulcan’s Throne, Ce 122 ppm in the olivine-corrected liquid) and 1.64 wt% (Cima, Ce proxy 62 ppm). The Sullivan Ranch inclusions support that range. Their H2O is close to undegassed: the deep CO2-rich vapor removes at most 0.2 wt%. Their H2O/Ce spans 149–416 (main group 149–331, median 215), which covers the literature range and extends above it, so 265 is not an extreme choice. One ratio times whole-rock Ce still does not predict Sullivan Ranch itself (265 × 85 ppm = 2.25 wt%, against 3.55), because there H2O varies with Cl, not Ce; (b) cpx/melt D against tetrahedral Al on the published scale, every study of the deposited panel (O’Leary 2010, Aubaud 2004 and 2008, Tenner 2009, Hauri 2006, Potts 2021 and 2022, Adam 2016; Curtolo 2025 open) with O’Leary eq. 10 at Ca = 0.67 (±21 %); (c) cpx core H2O against Cr (bars: total 1σ and the EMPA Cr standard deviation); (d) the 28 recalibrated experiments with the eq. 10 form refit to them (ln D = −4.19 + 4.92 IVAl − 1.24 Ca, ±20 %); (e) panel b with each D adjusted to the curve’s Ca, D × exp(−1.0 (0.67 − Ca)): adjusted values, for comparison with the curve.

Figure 15, 2026 form. Mean cpx cores against melt H2O, and observed against predicted cpx/melt D (Figure 9.3). Bars for Vulcan’s Throne and Cima run to the H2O/Ce soft maximum (see above).
The deposited host-melt H2O (2.6, 2.3 and 1.5 wt%) is superseded by 3.549, 2.29 and 1.29 wt%; Vulcan’s Throne’s 2.29 is the wettest of its three inclusions, and its soft maximum (3.23 wt%, from literature ratios) made the earlier bars asymmetric. The eq. 10 curves fix Ca (D depends on IVAl and Ca), so experiments at other Ca sit off the curve even where the equation fits them; no measured point is moved except in panel e. The Potts pigeonite runs were listed in two source tables and are plotted once. On a common SIMS scale (panel d) the xenolith cpx hold 1.2-2.6 times the water the recalibrated experiments predict; the deposited panel b compared recalibrated xenolith values with published experiments.
